With Alt already held when the drag begins, you drag a copy, as in Tinkercad: the shape stays where it is and the copy lands where you let go. Pressing Alt only on the way pauses snapping; the shape then follows the grid only. A copy, too, snaps only once you let go of Alt on the way. To switch snapping off for good, use the grid menu in the bottom right (“Encaixar em formas”) or the settings. For now only moving on the normal workplane snaps, not lifting and not resizing.

Two or more selected shapes are lined up with “Alinhar”: points appear around the selection for left, centre and right, front, centre and back, and top, centre and bottom. A click on a point moves all shapes there. If you first click one of the selected shapes, it stays in place and the others line up with it. A locked shape in the selection is that fixed shape by itself. Left, right, front, back, top and bottom go by the box round a shape; the centre of a triangle, a pentagon or a star is its own middle, so a hole centred on one sits in the middle of the shape and not of its box. A shape turned at an angle, say by 45°, has its box round it to line up with, not its own edges. To line up with the edges, set a workplane on a face of that shape first (“Posicionar plano de trabalho”, then click the face): the points then stand on the axes of that plane, and the shapes are measured and moved along them, as in Tinkercad. Reset the workplane to line up along the plate again. Align shows the possible targets as dots around the selection. The key is L. Esc cancels.

Hold Alt while aligning and the dots turn into squares: a click no longer moves the shapes but changes their size. A dot at a side stretches each shape to that side, its other side staying where it is, as if you had dragged its handle there. The dot in the middle leaves each shape in its place and gives it the width, length or height in that direction. That way you swap a box for a cylinder of the same size, say, or replace a broken piece of a mesh with a clean shape. Move over a dot with Alt held and you see beforehand how large the shapes become. The reference is the shape you clicked first; only the others change. Without one, the side dots stretch all shapes to the farthest side, and the middle dot gives them all the size of the largest. A cylinder stays round, so it grows in the other direction too. A shape turned at an angle stays as it is; shapes turned by 90° work.

“Espelhar” (M, or right-click the selection and choose it) flips the selection across a plane: “esquerda-direita”, “frente-trás” or “cima-baixo”. Click the matching axis arrow. That is handy for symmetric parts: build one half, copy it and mirror the copy.

You rotate with the curved arrows on the shape, with the numbers in the settings or with R in 45° steps. When you drag on the rotation circle, the turn snaps to every tick, that is every 22.5°; hold Shift for finer steps, and extra ticks appear every 11.25°. Drag outside the circle to turn freely in 1° steps, or in 45° steps with Shift. Normally the selection turns about its centre. Sometimes it should not, for example when a tilted tube is to be turned further at its end. For that there is “Definir ponto de rotação”: afterwards click on a face. A flat face supplies its centre, for example the axis of a tube end. On a group or a bundle the face runs on across parts that meet, as on one body, and the pivot goes to the middle of the whole face once the parts are joined, except on a group or bundle with text in it, or a bundle with a hole among its parts. The selection now turns about that point. A second click on the tool removes it again. The angles stay with the body. In its settings, “Rotação” shows them as “Em torno de X”, “Em torno de Y” and “Em torno de Z (altura)”, named like the position: Y runs across the plate, Z is up. Type an angle there and the body turns to it - about its centre, or about its own pivot if it has one. While a turned body is selected, its angles also show below it on the workplane; “Mostrar os ângulos de sólidos girados” in the settings switches that off. A body turned about two axes: its angles stand under it, and the Rotation card in its settings takes them as numbers. With one body selected, the pivot belongs to that body: select other parts and come back, and it is still there. It moves, turns and scales with the body, is saved in the project and comes back with Undo. Under “Posição” the pivot has its own X, Y and Z, which you can type or nudge, and “Remover” takes it away. You can also drag the pivot's red marker with the mouse: it slides over the surface of the bodies and snaps to corners, edge midpoints and edges, so a hinge pin lands exactly on a corner. With several bodies selected the pivot is only for that selection, and a new selection removes it. Grouping or bundling them keeps it: the group takes the pivot as its own, with X, Y and Z under “Posição”.

Should a part lie on its best side for printing? Select it, click “Deitar sobre a face” and then the face that should go down. While you move the pointer over the part, the face under it lights up, so you see which one you are about to pick; turn the view to check the other sides. The part turns so that this face rests on the workplane. Two parts should meet face to face, or line up flush? Select the part that should move, click “Alinhar faces”, then click its face and after that the face of the other part. In the panel, “Face com face” puts the faces against each other (back to back, touching), “Rente” lays them in one plane side by side; “Espaço” leaves room between them, for example for clearance. “Alinhar” moves the part: it turns the shortest way until the faces are parallel - not at all if they already are - and then slides only towards the other face, so it keeps its place sideways. The other part stays where it is, and one Undo takes it all back. The Align faces panel: the part that moves is picked, a face of the other part comes next, then face to face or flush, and an optional gap. Holes on one axis: “Mesmo eixo” lines up round faces instead: a hole over a hole, a pin in a hole, a screw in its clearance hole. Choose it before you click the faces. Then click the round inside of a hole (or the outside of a pin) on the part that moves, and a round face of the other part; the whole round face lights up while you point at it. “Alinhar” turns the part the shortest way until the two axes are parallel and slides it straight across onto the other axis. Along the axis it stays where it was, so a pin keeps its height; push it in afterwards. This works on imported meshes too, as long as the hole is made of facets around one axis. An exact angle between two faces: “Alinhar faces” leaves the faces parallel; there is no tool of its own for an angle between them, but this gets you there. First bring the faces together with “Alinhar faces”, so they are parallel. Then set the pivot on the edge where they meet (“Definir ponto de rotação”, click the edge or a corner) and type the angle, 15 or 30 say, in the “Rotação” card of the part. It turns about that pivot. The card's axes are the axes of the plate, so this works when the edge runs along X, Y or Z. Just as simple are “Baixar até o plano de trabalho” (D), which drops the selection onto the workplane, and “Centralizar no plano de trabalho”. With the workplane on a face, it centres on the point you picked with W and moves the selection only along that face, so what stands on it stays on it. C picks the selection up, like Cruise in Tinkercad: it follows the mouse pointer and lies down on the face of another body you are over, sloped ones too. A click sets it down there, Esc leaves it where it was. Its underside then rests on the face, lined up with the face's edges as a new shape would be; it keeps its own turn about its up axis. Several parts travel together and keep their spacing. Over the empty plate, C stands a tilted part upright on the workplane again. Without a keyboard, the menu of a long press has “Colocar sobre uma face” for the same.

For hole grids, bolt circles and rings of teeth there is the “Padrão”. Select the shapes to be multiplied and click it in the ribbon. The pattern in "Circle" mode: the copies first appear as a preview. “Fileira”: The selection is repeated at equal distances. The row steps along all three axes at once, with “Espaçamento X”, “Espaçamento Y” and “Espaçamento Z (altura)”: one of them gives a straight row, two or three a diagonal row or a staircase. A negative spacing lays the row the other way. “Círculo”: The selection is spread around a centre. How many copies there are you set under “Quantidade (com o original)”, and the “Ângulo total” is 360° for a full circle. Choose whether the copies turn along. “Subida por cópia” lifts every copy a little more than the one before (a screw or an ascending spiral), and “Mudança de raio por cópia” moves it further from the centre or closer to it (a flat spiral); together they give a conical spiral. A spiral winds once around at most: an angle above 360° counts as a full circle, and there are at most 100 copies. Tip: first set the pivot on a face with “Definir ponto de rotação”, then the centre of the circle lies exactly there. The pattern in "Circle" mode with a rise and a radius change per copy: the copies climb and widen like a spiral. The copies first appear as a preview. Only “Criar” creates them. If the copies are holes, group them afterwards with the body they should cut into. With “Agrupar cópias” ticked, “Criar” groups the original and all copies into one object in the same step, as “Grupo de união” would: a ring of 36 pieces is then one part you can move, colour or cut with. Above 5 pieces the box ticks itself; once you tick or untick it yourself, it stays as you set it. “Desagrupar” brings the pieces back. If grouping does not work out, the pattern still comes in as separate pieces and the message says why.

For vents, speaker grilles, baskets and enclosures the “Padrão de furos” spreads holes evenly over a flat face. You no longer have to make one hole, repeat it and set it onto the wall. Select exactly one body and click “Padrão de furos” in the “Modificar” group of the toolbar, next to the pattern. You can also right-click the body, or find it with Ctrl+K. Click a flat face of the body. The whole flat face around your click counts, not just the triangle under the pointer. A curved face does not work: you get a hint and click a flat one instead. On a group or a bundle a face runs on across parts that meet, as on one body; on a bundle only when no hole is among them. The parts are joined shortly after the tool opens; until then only one part's face lights up under the pointer, and a click waits for the join. On a group or bundle with text in it, only one part's face lights up, and the click joins the parts. In the window, set how the holes look and lie: “Forma do furo”: “Redondo”, “Quadrado”, “Retângulo”, “Hexágono” or “Oblongo”. Size: the “Diâmetro (Ø)” of a round hole, the “Comprimento do lado” of a square one, “Largura” and “Altura” for a rectangle and a slot. For the hexagon the size is the “Diâmetro entre cantos (Ø)”. “Espaçamento centro a centro”: the distance from one hole's middle to the next. If it is smaller than the holes allow, PrintCaddy raises it to the smallest possible value so a wall stays between the holes. For rectangles and slots it counts along the row, from left to right. “Rows centre to centre”: rectangles and slots only: the distance from one row to the next. So narrow, tall holes stand close side by side while the rows keep apart. A hole 2 mm wide and 14 mm high needs 4 mm along the row and 16 mm from row to row with a 2 mm wall. “Parede entre os furos”: the same distance said another way: the wall left between two neighbouring holes, which is the wall thickness in the print. Set it and the spacing centre to centre follows (for rectangles and slots the row spacing too), and the other way round. For hexagons, rectangles and slots PrintCaddy measures the least distance between their edges. “Disposição”: “Grade” puts the holes in rows and columns. “Intercalada” shifts every second row by half a spacing and moves the rows closer, so every hole has neighbours at the same distance - with hexagons that makes a honeycomb. “Margem até a borda da face”: the clear distance between the holes and the edge of the face. Only holes that lie wholly inside the face minus this margin are made; anything that would reach beyond it is left out. The margin also holds around openings in the face. “Profundidade”: “Atravessando o sólido inteiro” (the default) cuts through the whole wall. With “Profundidade personalizada” you give the depth in millimetres, for recesses, say. The holes show at once as a preview on the face and follow every value. The window says how many holes fit. “Outra face” chooses another face, Esc closes the tool, and like the other tool windows it moves by its title bar. Only “Criar” makes the holes. The holes are ordinary holes grouped with the body, just as after “Grupo de união”: nothing is baked in. “Desagrupar” dissolves the group again and frees every hole, which you can then move, change or delete one by one. The whole thing is one step for “Desfazer”. The tool does not make more than 400 holes at once; make the holes bigger or the spacing wider then. An AI can do the same through the MCP bridge with layerling_perforate_face (see the chapter AI with MCP).

h: Pushing a face out or in
t: For a thicker wall, a raised pad on a face or a pocket cut into it, the “Face” tool works on one flat face. It works on an imported STL too, where there is no sketch to change. Select exactly one body and click “Face” in the “Modificar” group of the toolbar, next to the hole pattern. You can also right-click the body, or find it with Ctrl+K. Click a flat face of the body. As with the hole pattern, the whole flat face around your click counts; a curved face does not work. On a group or a bundle the face runs on across parts that meet, as with the hole pattern. In the window: “Direção”: choose “Para fora: adicionar material” for material standing on the face or “Para dentro: cortar uma cavidade” for a pocket cut into it. A pocket goes no deeper than the body behind the face; on a hollow body it can still reach the cavity. “Recuo a partir da borda da face”: how far the new outline stays inside the face's edge. Going out, 0 takes the whole face, which makes a wall thicker. Openings in the face grow by the same amount. “Raio dos cantos”: rounds every corner of the outline, the inner ones too, so a sharp tip ends in an arc. A notch narrower than twice the radius closes, and a part of the face narrower than twice the inset and the radius together is left out. “Profundidade”: how far the new part stands out of the face, or how deep the pocket goes. “Como um sólido próprio (não agrupado)”: with the switch on, the new part (or the hole of a pocket) is a body of its own beside the body instead of a group with it, so you can resize it, move it or use it to cut at once. The result shows at once as a preview and follows every value. “Outra face” chooses another face, Esc closes the tool. Only “Criar” makes it. What the tool adds is an ordinary sketch body, grouped with the body unless “Como um sólido próprio (não agrupado)” is on (then “Editar grupo” has nothing to open, and the part is free): nothing is baked in. “Editar grupo” opens the group, and “Editar esboço” on the new part shows the outline it follows. On the top or the bottom of a plain sketch body - one area, not grouped, mirrored, tapered, twisted or leaning, and without a stroke, key ring, fillet or chamfer - that is the body's own outline, set in when it is built, so its lines and arcs stay exact wherever the CAD kernel can set them in, for the edge tools and the STEP export. Resized later, the part keeps its inset. On any other face, and on every face of an imported mesh, the outline follows the face's triangles, and a curve is made of short straight pieces. The whole thing is one step for “Desfazer”. To change the inset or the radius later, undo and run the tool again. To round the top edge afterwards, use “Arredondamento” with “Arestas de cima” on the group as the last step: like every edge treatment on a group, it joins the group into one body. An AI can do the same through the MCP bridge with layerling_push_face (see the chapter AI with MCP).

With several parts selected, the properties panel on the right shows how many there are and offers what applies to all of them together: “Sólido” or “Orifício”, one colour for all (a click on “Sólido” opens the colours) and the lock. With a mixed selection, one click makes them all solids or all holes. If any of the parts is locked, only the lock can be used. Sizes are changed with the handles, with “Redimensionar por porcentagem” or by typing a number into a size label. With several parts the number is the size of the whole selection: every part grows with it, the spaces between them too, as when you drag a handle. Solid and hole also work with a right-click or the S and H keys.

To make one or several parts larger or smaller by the same share, say all the parts of a print file by 20 %, use “Redimensionar por porcentagem”. Select the parts, right-click them and choose “Redimensionar por porcentagem”, or search for it with Ctrl+K. Under “Novo tamanho” you type the new size as a percentage of the current one: 120 % is a fifth larger, 50 % half the size. Width, depth and height change alike, so the proportions stay. The bottom stays where it is, so nothing sinks into the plate. With several parts you choose how they grow: “Juntas”: The parts grow around their common centre, and the gaps grow with them. The whole becomes larger as if it were one part. “Cada uma no lugar”: Every part grows where it stands, and the gaps between them stay the same. The percentage field has the focus when the window opens, so from the keyboard it is Ctrl+K, the percentage, Enter; Esc closes the window. Only “Redimensionar” (or Enter in the field) changes the design, and one step back undoes it. With a locked part in the selection it does not open.
“Desfazer” (Ctrl+Z) and “Refazer” (Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y) step through your history. How many steps travel with the saved design you set in the settings under “Histórico”.

“Histórico”, next to undo and redo, opens a view of your history without changing anything. The work area shows the design as it was, and a slider at the bottom runs through every undo step: all the way to the right is the current state, each step to the left is one undo earlier, and states you have undone sit to the right of the current one. The arrow keys step through the states, Esc returns to the current state. The mouse wheel over the slider does the same, one state per notch, up to an earlier one; Page Up and Page Down jump ten states, Home goes to the oldest state and End back to the current one. You can turn and zoom the view meanwhile and click objects to bring them back (see below), but nothing can be moved; the design itself stays exactly as it is. If the bar covers something, drag it away by its title bar; a double-click on it brings it back. Two things you can take along from an earlier state. “Novo projeto a partir deste estado” puts that state into a new design in the overview, named after this one with the time of that state in brackets - a design saved before PrintCaddy recorded times says "copy" instead - and with the history up to that point, so undo keeps working there. “Exportar este estado” opens the usual export with that state as the design, so you can save it as STL, 3MF, STEP, a picture or a LYL file with the history up to that state. You can also bring single objects back into the design. Click an object in the state shown - Shift+click adds more or takes one off again, a click on empty space picks nothing - and choose “Trazer para o projeto”. The view closes and a copy of each object lands in the current design exactly as it was in that state and at the spot it had there, selected, next to whatever the design holds now; nothing else changes. It is one step, so undo takes it back. Use it for a version of a part you changed since, or for one you deleted. A group comes back whole; notes and reference points on an object stay behind. Its name carries the time of that state, such as “Box (12:32)”, so it is easy to tell from the version the design has now. To bring back a part from inside a group, select the group and choose “Abrir grupo” or press E, as in the design: its parts are laid out where editing the group would put them, ready to pick, and the bar says which group you are in. “Sair” closes it again. This is only to look - the group, the design and the history stay as they are. “Excluir histórico” sits alone at the bottom left of the bar. After a question it removes every earlier step for good: the design keeps the state it has now (not the one shown), Undo has nothing to go back to and a file saved afterwards carries no history. Use it to share a design without its past, or to start the undo steps over. It cannot be undone; to share a file without touching your own design, choose “Nenhum” when exporting instead.

Como formas simples viram furos, rasgos e cavidades, e como alterar um grupo de união depois. Esta é a ideia mais importante do PrintCaddy, e ela se aprende rápido: toda forma é um sólido ou um orifício. Um sólido fica. Um orifício é uma ferramenta que tira material.

Selecione uma forma e clique em “Sólido” ou “Orifício” no painel de propriedades. Pelo teclado é mais rápido: H transforma a seleção em orifício, S a transforma de novo em sólido. As duas opções também estão no menu que aparece com um clique direito no sólido. Um orifício aparece transparente, para você ver onde ele está. T deixa um sólido transparente, por exemplo para olhar dentro de uma carcaça; pressione T de novo para deixá-lo opaco. Com vários sólidos selecionados, T vale para todos: se pelo menos um já estiver transparente, todos ficam opacos; se nenhum estiver, todos ficam transparentes. Enquanto nada estiver agrupado, um orifício não faz nada. Ele só fica ali e mostra onde algo vai sumir depois. O cilindro é um orifício. Ele sai pelo topo do cubo, para atravessá-lo de ponta a ponta.

Selecione os sólidos e os orifícios e clique em “Grupo de união” (Ctrl+G). Agora os orifícios tiram o material dos sólidos em que tocam. O que sobra é uma única forma nova. O resultado: um cubo com um furo. É assim que se fazem: Furos: um cilindro como orifício atravessando um sólido. Rasgos: uma caixa alongada como orifício na borda. Cavidades: um orifício que não atravessa até o outro lado. Roscas numa peça: um furo roscado como orifício, veja Roscas e mecânica. Se houver vários sólidos no grupo de união, eles se juntam. Dois sólidos que se tocam viram uma única peça. Com malhas grandes, como um STL importado com centenas de milhares de triângulos, o corte leva alguns segundos. PrintCaddy então trabalha em segundo plano e mostra "“Calculando… você pode continuar trabalhando”"; enquanto isso, você pode girar a vista e usar a interface. Se você alterar o modelo nesse meio-tempo, o resultado é descartado e PrintCaddy avisa. O mesmo vale para “Dividir”. Um grupo de união pode ser tratado como uma forma: mover, girar, mudar a cor, agrupar de novo. “Desagrupar” (Ctrl+Shift+G) desfaz o grupo de união, e as peças voltam a ficar separadas.

h: Transformando um grupo de união em orifício
t: Um grupo de união inteiro também pode ser um sólido ou um orifício. Vale uma regra simples: Se o grupo de união tem só sólidos (ou só orifícios), você o troca por inteiro e as peças acompanham. Se tem os dois, por exemplo um cubo com um furo, cada peça mantém o seu próprio estado. O grupo de união inteiro vira então uma ferramenta, mas o furo continua sendo um furo.

Às vezes as peças só devem ficar juntas, sem virar uma só, por exemplo um logotipo branco sobre uma placa preta para uma impressão multicolorida. É para isso que serve “Criar conjunto” (Ctrl+B), como no Tinkercad. Um conjunto se move, gira e muda de tamanho como uma forma, mas nada é fundido: Cada peça mantém a sua cor e continua sendo um sólido ou um orifício. No painel de propriedades, o conjunto tem os mesmos cartões de um grupo de união: “Sólido” e “Orifício” para o conjunto inteiro (que mantêm as cores das peças), “Transparente” (T) e “Multicor” (Shift+M); com “Multicor” desligado, o conjunto aparece e é exportado numa cor só. “Separar peças” desfaz o conjunto, como Ctrl+Shift+G. Os orifícios não cortam nada. Quando você agrupa o conjunto com outras peças, os orifícios dele cortam essas peças, mas continuam sem cortar os sólidos do próprio conjunto, como no Tinkercad. Assim, por exemplo, um pino com o seu orifício ao lado pode ser reaproveitado várias vezes como conjunto. Ao exportar em STL, 3MF ou OBJ, cada peça é um sólido separado; em 3MF e OBJ, com a sua cor. “Desagrupar” (Ctrl+Shift+G) desfaz um conjunto, e E o abre para edição, como um grupo de união. Chanfro, arredondamento e vazar não funcionam num conjunto, porque ele não é um único sólido: para isso, agrupe-o ou trabalhe nas peças uma por uma. Se um orifício do conjunto também deve cortar os sólidos do próprio conjunto, desfaça o conjunto e agrupe as peças (Ctrl+G).

“Interseção booleana” mantém só o que dois ou mais sólidos têm em comum. Coloque duas formas uma sobre a outra, sobrepostas, selecione as duas e clique em “Interseção booleana”. Assim um cilindro e uma caixa viram uma peça com um lado redondo e um lado reto. Um grupo de união entra na interseção do jeito que aparece, com os orifícios já recortados. Se um orifício também estiver selecionado, o que sobra é o que todos os sólidos têm em comum com todos os orifícios. Se as formas não têm nada em comum, uma mensagem informa que nada foi alterado. Ao lado de “Interseção booleana”, o botão “Mostrar parte em comum” exibe a parte em comum antes de você aplicá-la: as formas selecionadas ficam transparentes, e o que elas têm em comum aparece em verde. Selecione e mova cada forma separadamente, e a parte verde acompanha; “Interseção booleana” aplica, Esc fecha a prévia. “Envoltória” envolve as formas selecionadas em um único sólido convexo, como se fossem embaladas a vácuo: o menor sólido sem reentrâncias que contém todas elas. Uma meia esfera sobre um cilindro vira uma cúpula sem degrau, quatro cilindros nos cantos viram uma caixa de cantos arredondados, e duas esferas, uma cápsula. Os orifícios da seleção são recortados da envoltória depois. A envoltória guarda as peças: “Editar grupo” a abre como um grupo de união, e se você mover uma peça dentro dela e clicar em “Concluído”, a envoltória é reconstruída. A envoltória é uma malha, então formas redondas mostram facetas, e as ferramentas de aresta funcionam nela como em qualquer malha.

Para peças que precisam encaixar, um eixo em uma bucha ou um parafuso em uma caixa, você faz uma peça e a recorta da outra. Selecione os dois sólidos e clique em “Recortar” na área “Combinar”, ou dê um clique direito e escolha “Recortar” no menu. O painel nomeia a peça que é mantida e o sólido que recebe a cavidade; PrintCaddy escolhe o menor como peça, e “Trocar os dois” inverte. “Folga” deixa a cavidade maior que a peça nessa medida, de cada lado: com 0, o encaixe é exato; 0,2 mm é uma folga comum para um encaixe impresso. “Recortar” recorta uma cópia da peça do outro sólido e deixa a própria peça onde está. O resultado é um grupo de união: “Desagrupar” separa o recorte de novo. Uma folga exige que a peça seja um sólido exato, como na ferramenta “Deslocamento”, que o recorte usa para isso.

Se um furo ficou pequeno demais, você não precisa desfazer o grupo de união e montar tudo de novo. Selecione o grupo de união e clique em “Editar grupo” no painel de propriedades, no ícone de pasta na lista de objetos, ou pressione E. Um clique duplo no grupo de união faz o mesmo, como no Tinkercad, e num conjunto também; se preferir que não, desligue “Clique duplo abre um grupo de união ou um conjunto” nas configurações. Uma peça só começa a se mover depois que o ponteiro foi arrastado alguns pixels, então um clique ou clique duplo tremido não a desloca. As peças agora ficam separadas, e você as altera com qualquer ferramenta: aumentar um orifício, mover um sólido, adicionar um orifício. O grupo de união em edição: a barra embaixo tem Cancelar e Concluído, e a lista de objetos mostra as peças. Uma barra aparece na parte de baixo da área de trabalho. “Concluído” reconstrói o grupo de união, com o nome, a cor e o estado de sólido ou orifício. “Cancelar” o devolve sem alterações. Se uma das peças for ela mesma um grupo de união, você pode editá-la do mesmo jeito, e assim por diante, até onde o seu projeto for. A barra mostra onde você está, por exemplo "Suporte › Ressalto do parafuso". “Concluído” e “Cancelar” sempre concluem o grupo de união mais interno e levam você um nível para fora. Enquanto você está dentro de um grupo de união, só os grupos de união entre as peças dele podem ser editados; para editar outro, conclua primeiro. Ao contrário de “Desagrupar”, que desfaz um grupo de união de vez, editar mantém o grupo: o nome e as configurações ficam, e você sempre pode voltar com “Cancelar”. Uma observação: arredondamentos e chanfros que você aplicou no grupo de união inteiro se perdem na reconstrução. A barra mostra esse aviso.

“Dividir”, na área “Modificar”, corta a seleção em duas com um plano, por exemplo uma peça grande demais para a mesa de impressão, ou uma cujo interior você quer ver. Selecione um ou mais sólidos ou orifícios e clique em “Dividir”. Um plano translúcido mostra exatamente onde o corte vai passar, e uma linha branca o marca nos próprios sólidos, onde o plano os encontra; nada muda até você aplicar. “Orientação do plano”: X faz um corte vertical entre esquerda e direita, Y entre frente e trás, Z um corte horizontal entre cima e baixo. Os eixos têm os mesmos nomes do cartão Posição, com Z para cima. O plano começa paralelo ao plano de trabalho, então na mesa com Z. “Alinhar ao plano de trabalho”: “Paralelo” deita o plano paralelo ao plano de trabalho, “Transversal a X” e “Transversal a Y” o deixam em pé, perpendicular a ele, atravessando a direção X ou Y dele. Onde a origem do plano de trabalho cruza a seleção, o plano passa por essa origem; senão, pelo meio. Assim você coloca o plano de trabalho numa face inclinada com W e corta bem ali, sem mexer nos controles deslizantes. “Posição do plano”: onde o plano cruza, pelo controle deslizante ou digitando o valor. Ele começa no meio. Você também pode arrastar a ponta da seta no plano; o plano se move ao longo da seta em incrementos de 0,1 mm. “Escolher face”, o botão ao lado da posição, deita o plano sobre uma face: clique nele e depois na face. Orientação, as duas rotações e a posição são ajustadas para combinar. Enquanto você escolhe, um plano azul sob o ponteiro mostra a face que será usada. Uma face de um sólido que não está selecionado também serve, para alinhar o corte com ela, mas o plano fica dentro da seleção. Esc interrompe a escolha e deixa o plano onde estava. Os dois controles deslizantes de rotação abaixo giram o plano em torno dos outros dois eixos, até 180° para cada lado, para um corte em ângulo. Eles podem ser combinados. “Dividir modelo” ou Enter faz o corte, Esc cancela (enquanto você escolhe uma face, o primeiro Esc só interrompe a escolha). Cada objeto que o plano cruza vira dois sólidos fechados, com o nome do seu lado, por exemplo "Caixa (Z+)" e "Caixa (Z-)"; os objetos que ele não cruza ficam como estão. Um orifício vira dois orifícios, e um sólido vazado mantém o seu espaço interno. As duas metades ficam onde estavam; para imprimir, deite cada uma sobre a face cortada com “Deitar sobre a face”. As metades são malhas simples: configurações como os lados de um cilindro ou as letras de um texto se perdem, então ajuste isso antes. Ctrl+Z traz o original de volta num só passo. Objetos bloqueados e ocultos não podem ser divididos. Uma malha importada precisa de uma superfície fechada para ser dividida, agrupada ou recortada. Se ela tiver aberturas, como os olhos de uma figura deixados abertos ou uma rachadura num escaneamento, PrintCaddy as fecha antes com uma tampa plana e diz quantas fechou. Ele fecha qualquer abertura pequena e qualquer abertura plana, seja do tamanho que for; uma abertura grande cuja borda não está toda no mesmo plano fica por sua conta, e a mensagem avisa. Feche-a no programa de onde o modelo veio, ou com uma ferramenta de reparo de malha, e importe de novo.

Se uma forma é composta de vários pedaços separados, como um texto feito de letras soltas, “Separar peças” a divide em formas independentes. A opção também está no menu que aparece com um clique direito na forma. Dica: Faça os orifícios sempre um pouco mais compridos que a peça que eles devem atravessar. Se o orifício termina exatamente rente à face, às vezes sobra uma película finíssima. Um milímetro a mais garante o corte.
Chamfer and fillet on chosen edges, walls of equal thickness for boxes, cups and cases.

Sharp edges rarely look good on a printed part, and they are not particularly strong either. A chamfer cuts the edge off at an angle, a fillet rounds it. Both act on the edges you click. Select the body (or the group). Click “Arredondamento” or “Chanfro” in the ribbon, press B for the fillet or Shift+B for the chamfer, or right-click the body and pick it from the menu. The body's edges light up. Click those that should be affected. Another click takes an edge out again. With Shift you add or remove a single edge. Set the size and confirm with “Aplicar” or Enter. Afterwards the window stays open on the new body with the same size, so the next fillet or chamfer can follow at once; “Concluído”, Esc or the cross closes it. With Shift or Ctrl a click on “Arestas de cima”, “Arestas de baixo”, “Arestas verticais” or “Arestas horizontais” adds those edges to the ones picked instead of replacing them. The "Fillet edges" tool: all sharp edges are selected, the picture shows the preview with a 4 mm radius. The panel sits at the top right. If it covers edges you want to click, drag it away by its title bar; it opens there next time too, and so do “Vazar” and “Padrão”. Double-click the title bar to put it back. Picking a shape from the shape list while the panel is open closes it without applying anything, and the edges you clicked are forgotten. The click then places the new shape instead of picking edges. In the panel you find: “Todas as arestas vivas” selects every edge at once, “Limpar” empties the selection. “Raio” for the fillet. For the chamfer you set “Distância” or “Ângulo”. “Raio variável” (fillet only) lets the radius change along one edge: small at one end, larger at the other, evenly in between, as where a straight wall meets a slanted one. Click a single edge, then set “Raio no início” and “Raio no fim”. Which end counts as the start follows from how the edge was built; if the larger radius comes out at the wrong end, “Trocar as pontas” turns it round. It works on one edge at a time, so round several edges one after the other. “Editar” brings both values back. “Limite de aresta viva” decides which edges count as sharp at all. A value of 25° treats only clear kinks as edges and leaves flat transitions alone. “Arestas verticais” picks the edges that stand straight up, such as the corners of a box: one fillet then rounds all the vertical corners at once. “Arestas de cima” picks only the edges along the very top of the body. It is the quick way for a cookie cutter: build the outline in a sketch as a stroke, then chamfer the top edges. “Ângulo” sets how steep the chamfer is; it cannot reach further than the wall is thick. “Arestas de baixo” picks only the edges along the very bottom of the body, the mirror of “Arestas de cima”. It is the quick way to round or chamfer only the foot of a part. “Chanfro com arredondamento”, chosen at the top of the chamfer window next to “Chanfro”, makes the printable foot of a part: a chamfer at the plate that blends tangentially into a fillet toward the wall, so the first layers need no support and the edge still ends soft. “Distância” is the height the foot takes up, “Ângulo” (15° to 75°) the steepness of the chamfer at the plate. Pick the edges with “Arestas de baixo”. “Só arestas visíveis” hides the edges that lie behind the body from where you look. By default every edge shows through the body, which gets confusing on a busy part; with the switch on you see, and can click, only the edges facing you. Turn the view to reach the others. An edge drawn in red (see below) always shows. “Um clique também escolhe arestas que continuam suavemente”: a click then also picks edges that flow smoothly into each other, for example all edges around a face with rounded corners. The switch only decides what a click picks: the CAD kernel always carries a chamfer or fillet on along such smoothly continuing edges. The panel tells you along how many more edges that happens. “Manter o tamanho da aresta ao redimensionar” keeps the chamfer or fillet as large as it is, even if you scale the body later. “Qualidade da prévia” (“Rascunho”, “Padrão” or “Fina”) decides how finely the preview is calculated. For difficult parts “Rascunho” is faster. While you adjust the size, PrintCaddy recalculates the preview. It can take a moment. You may keep adjusting; the last value you chose is what gets calculated. If the size is too large for the edge, PrintCaddy says so and suggests a smaller value. Often one or two millimetres less will do. At sharp angles a fillet needs more room than its radius suggests. On a small screen the panel scrolls down by itself so the message is in view. When a selection that worked fails after you click one more edge, that edge turns red and is drawn wider: it is the one that cannot be treated together with the others at this size. Click it again to take it out, or make the size smaller. If you click more edges while the message stands, the first one stays red. When there is no earlier selection that worked - the very first click, or a size you just raised - the edges that fail even on their own turn red, or all of them if it is only their combination. The edge under the pointer is drawn wider too, so you can see which one a click will pick.

A treated body can always be treated again. Select it again and open the tool - Fillet, Chamfer or Hollow, each shows the list: under “Desfazer um tratamento de aresta” you see what is already on it. “Desfazer” takes back a single treatment. Note: if newer treatments lie on top, they go with it, and the panel tells you how many. Next to a chamfer, a fillet or a hollowing there is also “Editar”. It takes the treatment back the same way, but opens the tool again at once with the same edges and the old value. You change the value and apply it again: a 3 mm fillet becomes a 5 mm one without clicking the edges once more. If newer treatments lie on top, they go with it here too. This holds for edge treatments you make from now on; older ones only offer taking back, and so do single parts of a group. On a group, say a cylinder with a hole, the treated edge belongs to the finished body, not to one of its parts. So the group becomes a single body. “Desagrupar” still works on it: it takes the edge features back first and then dissolves the group, in one step that Ctrl+Z undoes. Take the treatment back as described above and the group returns with all its parts. The easiest way is to treat edges last. That goes for threads too: the edge tool takes a thread as its exact body, so a block with a tapped hole in it gets its edges rounded with the thread in place. Working out a thread's edges takes longer than for a plain shape, a few seconds for an M6 and about half a minute for a G1/2 pipe thread. Good to know: PrintCaddy works with real CAD geometry for fillets and chamfers, not just a triangle mesh. That is why a rounded edge is still a rounded edge in the STEP export. A part imported as STEP keeps its CAD geometry too: chamfers, fillets and hollowing work on the body from the file, however finely the part is drawn on screen. STL, OBJ and 3MF bring only triangles, and a finely drawn part can be too dense for the edge tool. If a part is also available as STEP, import that.

Boxes, cups, cases and covers have one thing in common: they are empty inside, with walls of equal thickness. That is exactly what “Vazar” does. Select the body and click “Vazar”, or right-click the body and pick it from the menu. Set the “Espessura da parede”. Under “Lados abertos”, switch on the sides that stay open: “Em cima”, “Embaixo”, “Frente”, “Trás”, “Esquerda” or “Direita”, as many as you like - “Frente” alone makes a slot for a drawer, “Esquerda” and “Direita” a tunnel. With no side switched on the body stays closed all round, with a cavity in the middle. “Fechado (cavidade interna)” switches every side off in one click. “Em cima” is already on when the panel opens; a click on it closes the top again. A body closed all round looks unchanged from outside: the section view shows the cavity. Decide whether the “Arestas internas” should be “Arredondadas” or “Vivas”. Click “Vazar”. The hollowing panel with wall thickness, a switch for each side that stays open, and the inner edges. The walls grow inward. The outside stays as it is. The “Arestas internas” only matter where the inner walls move apart - at a step in the body or around an opening. The corners of the cavity of a plain box are always sharp, with both settings. For a rounded inside, round the outside edges of the body first (see above), then hollow it: the inside follows with the radius minus the wall thickness. If the rounded inside cannot be built, which can happen with an outline made of very many short straight pieces such as a traced drawing, PrintCaddy builds the same hollow body with sharp inner corners instead. The result: a shell with a 3 mm wall, open at the top. The same box with only the front side open: a slot for a drawer. For every open side, the body needs a flat face at its very edge on that side. Spheres and free-form shapes therefore cannot be hollowed this way. If the wall is too thick for the body, PrintCaddy tells you and asks for a thinner one. A rounded box whose top and bottom edges are rounded as well is such a case: its wall has to be clearly thinner than that rounding, or set the rounding to 0 first. A body with a pocket - a block with a hole that does not go all the way through, made by grouping a box with a raised hole - can be hollowed too, with the top open: the walls round the pocket are hollowed as well, so a ring of cavity stays between the outer wall and the pocket, open at the top, and a thin cavity lies under the pocket's floor. Bodies that end in a point, such as a cone or a revolved triangle, have no flat face on top that could stay open. A fully closed cavity does not work there either, because a point cannot be offset inwards: even with a 1 mm wall you get the message that the walls cannot be this thick. Draw the wall into the profile before revolving instead: duplicate the outline, scale the copy down evenly, put it in the middle of the large outline and cut the large one with it, then revolve the whole (chapter Sketches, section Revolve). The distance between the two outlines is the wall thickness. If you resize a hollowed body later, PrintCaddy hollows it again at the new size right away. The wall stays as thick as you chose, round bodies included. A cylinder you pull further one way than the other becomes an ellipse. Fillets and chamfers you laid on it after the hollowing go on again at the same edges. Tip: With a 0.4 mm nozzle, 1.2 to 2 mm of wall is a good start: thin enough to save material, thick enough for a sturdy part.

Every face of a body can be moved by the same distance, out or in. That is what a press fit, a lid or a snap joint needs: a gap of 0.1 to 0.3 mm all round while the features stay where they are, which scaling cannot give you. Select one body and click “Deslocamento”, or right-click the body and choose it there. Choose “Aumentar” or “Diminuir” and set the “Distância”. The “Cantos externos” decide the outer corners: rounded keeps the offset surface round there, sharp lets the faces run on until they meet. Tick “Manter o original e adicionar o corpo deslocado como furo” to keep the part as it is and get the grown body as a copy that already is a hole. Group that hole with the mating part and it cuts exactly the clearance you chose. Click “Deslocar”. Without the tick the body itself is offset. It becomes a fixed exact body, like after a chamfer: the list at the top of the panel takes the offset back, and “Editar” opens the tool again with the old distance. Only bodies that are exact CAD bodies can be offset - boxes, cylinders and the other shapes, groups of them, imported STEP parts. A body that is only a triangle mesh, such as many STL imports, often cannot be. A distance that is too big for the body, for example a shrink beyond its thinnest wall, is refused.

A fillet in the way, a hole in the wrong place, a boss you no longer need: “Excluir face” takes it off the body again, without building the body anew. Select the body and click “Excluir face”, or right-click the body and pick it from the menu. Click every face of what should go: the faces of a rounded edge, the wall of a hole, the side and the top of a boss. A picked face lights up; another click takes it out again. The panel counts the faces. Click “Excluir” or press Delete. Esc closes the tool without changing anything. The faces around the deleted ones grow until the gap is closed. A box with rounded top edges gets its sharp edges back, a hole is filled, a boss is gone. The body stays exact, so it can be filleted and chamfered again and the STEP export keeps its true faces. Ctrl+Z takes the deletion back in one step. It is also listed under “Desfazer um tratamento de aresta” with the fillets and chamfers, where “Desfazer” takes it back; there is no “Editar” for it. On a group, the result is a single body, as with an edge treatment. Pick all the faces of what should go, and only those. If the faces around them cannot close the gap, PrintCaddy says so and nothing changes: a main side of a box, for example, has no neighbour that could take its place. Deleting only the floor of a pocket turns it into a hole straight through, because the walls of the pocket run on to the other side. “Excluir face” needs exact faces: it works on parts imported as STEP and on PrintCaddy's shapes. Whatever PrintCaddy keeps as a mesh has none: an imported STL, OBJ or 3MF, a split, wrapped or simplified body, or a very detailed shape such as a long text. Import a part as STEP if you can. On a detailed imported part, a few faces can be too much for the CAD kernel: after 45 seconds the deletion is stopped and nothing changes. A body resized after an edge treatment while keeping its edge size has no exact faces at its new size until the resize is taken back.

Draw a flat outline, round or chamfer its corners and pull or spin it into a body. Not everything can be put together from basic shapes. For parts with a contour of their own, such as a bracket, a tooth profile or a vase, you first draw the outline and then make a body from it. That is what sketch mode is for.

At the top, switch from “Editor 3D” to “Esboço”. In the “Criar” group of the ribbon, three buttons stand side by side for what the outline should become: “Extrusão do esboço”: The outline is pulled upward, like a cookie cutter. “Revolução do esboço”: The outline is spun about an axis, as on a lathe. That gives vases, cups, cones and everything round. “Varredura do esboço”: The outline is pulled along a path: a cable channel that turns a corner, a conduit, a ring round a shape. See Sweeping along a path below. The editor then shows a sheet with a grid. That is your drawing surface.

The ribbon in sketch mode is divided into areas: Draw: “Linha” makes straight sections: click points one after another; holding Shift snaps the new line in 15° steps, horizontal and vertical included. The length and angle of the new line show at the pointer. You can also type how long it should be, see Lines by numbers. “Arco” draws a true circular arc through three points: click its two ends first, then a third point the arc runs through; until that third click a preview follows the pointer, and the message names the radius. An end clicked on an existing point joins it, so an arc can close an outline. Esc drops the points clicked so far and goes back to “Selecionar”. After that the arc is ordinary geometry made of points and curves: move, cut or erase it like any other line. The “Curva de Bézier” is shaped with its handles: click a point and drag in the direction the line should carry on, as with the pen tool in Illustrator or Inkscape. The further you drag, the more it bends; the stretch to the new point bends along while you drag, so you see what you get. Dragging while you place a point bends the curve; if you come from Tinkercad and just want to click points, take the “Curva suave”. The “Curva suave” lays a flowing path through the points you click. To close the outline, click the first point again at the end. To end the chain of lines without closing the outline, right-click without moving the pointer, or double-click the last point. Shapes: “Adicionar forma ao esboço” offers ready-made outlines: “Retângulo”, “Círculo”, “Oval”, “Semicírculo”, “Fatia”, “Furos em círculo” (a disc with holes), “Triângulo”, “Hexágono”, a “Polígono” and a “Estrela”. Click one to put it at the origin of the sketch, or drag it from the menu to where you want it. At the bottom of the menu, “Lados / pontas” sets the number of sides of the polygon and of points of the star, and “Medida interna da estrela” how deep the star's valleys reach in towards the middle (10 to 90 percent of the outer radius); both apply to the next shape you add. Like every sketch shape they are ordinary corner points afterwards, so you can move, round or chamfer them one by one. Overlapping: Push two closed outlines over each other and they stay two bodies, which merge in the 3D editor; the overlap is not a hole. A hole only comes from an outline lying wholly inside another. Moving does not join the lines where they cross, so you can pull the shapes apart again. If you draw a line across others, though, PrintCaddy puts a point at every crossing. Selection: “Selecionar” moves points and lines. A click inside a closed outline selects the whole outline, so you can drag or resize it straight away; inside a hole it picks the hole. The frame around the selection has eight handles: the corners change width and height together, keeping the proportions while you hold Shift. The ones on the sides change one direction only. “Manter proporções” in the bar that appears keeps the proportions without Shift: the corners and sides then stretch both ways alike, and a typed width or height changes the other one too. PrintCaddy remembers the switch. “Bloquear” next to it locks the selected outline, like a locked body in the 3D editor (Ctrl+L does the same): it can no longer be moved, resized, turned or changed, its lines turn paler and its points grey, and the frame's handles turn grey and no longer respond. While it is selected, a padlock in its corner unlocks it with a click. Lines may still start at its corners. “Desbloquear” or Ctrl+L again frees it. The curved arrows beyond the corners of the frame turn the whole selection about its middle: the figure over the pointer shows the angle, and with Shift held it moves in steps of 15°. While you turn, a ring appears: with the pointer inside it the turn snaps to 22.5°, outside it goes in whole degrees, whatever the grid. R turns a whole closed outline by 45° at each press. Click the width or height pill to type a new size, also as a sum ("60+12.5") or in percent ("150%"). With Shift held, a click on a point or line adds it to the selection or takes it away again, so you can pick several and move them together. Drag a box over empty space to select everything in it. With two or more outlines selected, the bar also lines them up: left, centred or right, and top, centred or bottom, on the frame round all of them. Each outline moves as a whole and keeps its shape; centred both ways, two circles become a ring. A locked outline stays where it is, and the others line up on it. A line can be dragged too (it moves by its two ends, or all of the selection if it is part of one). The arrow keys move the selection by one grid step, Shift with them by a larger one, and Shift held while you drag keeps the move on one axis. “Adicionar ou remover pontos”: a click on a section adds a point, a click on a point removes it. Also there are “Apagar” (a click on a point or line takes it away, a window dragged over several takes away everything inside it, and with something selected the button erases the selection) and inserting a template image (“Adicionar imagem”). When you remove a point, PrintCaddy joins its two neighbours so the outline stays closed. To close a gap, for example after erasing one side of a hexagon, drag one open end onto the other: it snaps there and the two become one point, so the outline is closed again. At a crossing, such as where a line cuts a circle, the sides that run straight on are joined: arc with arc, line with line, and the circle stays round. To get rid of only a piece of a circle, for a rounded corner say, click exactly that piece of arc between two points with the eraser; the rest stays. Clipboard: “Copiar”, “Colar”, “Duplicar” and “Excluir” work on the selected points, lines and images, as in the 3D editor; Ctrl+X cuts. Pasted and duplicated geometry lands next to the original with a 10 mm gap, on a free spot where it touches no existing line, so it never gets joined to what is already there. It stays selected, so you can drag it straight into place. History: “Desfazer no esboço” and “Refazer no esboço”. Manage: “Anotação” (or N) puts a note on the sketch, as in the 3D editor: the next click places it, anywhere, on a line too. Drag the pin to move it; a click on the pin folds the card away. The notes of a sketch belong to its body: in the 3D view they sit on top of an extruded or swept body and on the drawn profile of a revolved one, and they move with it. Opening the sketch again shows all of the body's notes, those placed in 3D too. “Desfazer no esboço” takes back a note like a line, and “Cancelar” discards what changed in the notes. More in the chapter Measuring and notes. View: Pan it with the middle mouse button or with Shift or Ctrl plus the right mouse button, as in the 3D editor. With nothing selected, Ctrl and the arrow keys slide it too: a tenth of the view a press, half with Shift as well; the sketch moves the way they point. Home fits the whole sketch in the view, F zooms to the selection (with nothing selected, to the whole sketch), and + and − zoom in and out, as in the 3D editor. With nothing selected, a double-click on an empty spot slides the view so that the spot comes to the middle, as in the 3D editor; “Clique duplo no plano de trabalho centraliza a vista ali” in the settings switches that off. The “Trena” on the side bar measures the distance between two points. The sketch also shows dimensions as soon as you click something: the length of a line, or for a point the lengths of the lines that meet there. The “Mostrar medidas” button on the side bar hides and shows these dimensions when they get in the way, for example while shaping curves; the tape measure keeps working. On a straight line you can click the dimension pill and type the length in millimetres; Enter applies it, Esc cancels. The line keeps its direction, its start point stays where it is, and the lines at the other end follow. With an end point selected, that one moves. Alt+Enter grows the line to both sides around its middle. On curves the pill only shows the length. A body comes only from a closed outline. An L-shaped outline. At the selected corner point, top left, the lengths of the two lines are shown in millimetres, and the angle between them in degrees. The keys 1 to 4 pick the drawing tools, in the order of the bar: “Linha”, “Curva de Bézier”, “Curva suave” and “Adicionar ou remover pontos”. They work as long as no line is being drawn; while one is, the digits are its length (see below). With the “Selecionar” tool and lines or points selected, the same keys change them instead: 1 makes lines straight and points corners, 2 turns lines into curves and 3 makes points smooth. With nothing selected they pick the tool as before.

Once you have set the first point with “Linha” or “Curva suave”, just type a number: two fields open next to the line, “Comprimento” in millimetres and “Ângulo” in degrees. < or Tab moves to the angle, so "50<30" gives a line 50 mm long at 30°, as in AutoCAD. Enter sets the point, and you can type the next line straight away; Esc closes the fields without ending the line chain. The angle counts counterclockwise from the right: 0° to the right, 90° up, 180° to the left, 270° down. Leave it empty and the line follows the pointer, so you give only the length and show the direction with the mouse. Sums like "40+12.5" work in both fields. If the point would land off the plate, the field says so and waits for another value.

Select a straight line and click “Curvar linha” in the bar that appears: the side bows out into a curve, as in Tinkercad, and shows its two handles. Drag them to shape the curve; the further out a handle stands, the stronger the bend. “Linha reta” makes the side straight again. A point you select can be made round with “Curva suave”: it gets handles of its own and the lines next to it become curves. With three or more points selected, “Curva por pontos” in the bar lays one flowing curve from the first of them to the last, through every point in between, the way the “Curva suave” tool draws one; the lines beyond the two ends stay as they are. Other programs call this "Fit curve" or "Fit point spline". The two differ: “Curvar linha” bends each selected side on its own and keeps the corners between them, for an arch on one side; “Curva por pontos” runs one curve through the points with no corners left, for smoothing a jagged traced edge. Click a handle and it lights up: the arrow keys then move it by one grid step, with Shift by a larger step, so you can set a curve precisely. The bottom side of the L-shaped outline bent into a curve, with its two handles at the ends.

Click a corner point where two straight lines meet: next to the lengths, PrintCaddy shows the angle between them in degrees, with a small arc. On a closed outline it is the angle inside the shape, so a dent reads above 180°. Click the value and type a new angle. One of the two lines then turns about the corner and keeps its length, and the other stays where it is. The line that turns is drawn dashed; Tab switches to the other one, Enter applies and Esc cancels. What hangs at the far end of the turned line goes with it. Moving a point changes three angles: at the point itself and at the two neighbouring corners at the far ends of its lines. So PrintCaddy shows those two as well, and each can be clicked and typed. That way you set, say, the bottom left corner to 75.5° while the top left point, which moves for it, is selected. You can calculate here too, e.g. "90-14.5". A corner shows no angle where a curve meets it, or where more than two lines meet. The “Mostrar medidas” button on the side bar hides the angle together with the lengths.

Click a corner point and choose “Arredondar canto” or “Chanfrar canto”. A small field appears for the “Raio” or the “Distância”. Enter the size and confirm with the check mark. This works for corners between two straight lines. Several corners at once work too: select them with Shift and a click each, or pull a frame round them, and choose “Arredondar canto” or “Chanfrar canto” from the bar that appears. All of them get the same radius or distance. Where two selected corners share a side, each takes at most 45 % of it, so a rectangle rounded all round comes out alike at every corner. Points that are not a corner between two straight lines are left out, and the message says how many. A frame round a whole shape, or a click inside it, selects its corners and its lines together, and the bar then offers “Curvar linha” and “Linha reta” for all the selected lines next to the corner tools. The corner at the top left is rounded with a 12 mm radius.

Select points and lines (click, Shift and click, or pull a frame round them) and click “Espelhar” in the bar. Then choose the axis: “Esquerda-direita” mirrors across the vertical axis through the middle of the plate, “Cima-baixo” across the horizontal one, and “Por uma linha” across a straight line of the sketch that you click next. The copy is added on the other side and the original stays; nothing is linked, so you can change either on its own. Points that lie on the axis are shared, so a half outline whose ends sit on the axis becomes one closed outline: draw half of a bracket, select it, mirror it and make the body. A construction line makes a good axis. Esc cancels.

A construction line helps you place points without becoming part of the body. It is drawn dashed and never counts as outline: you can pull it as far beyond the shape as you like and the body does not grow. Switch on “Linha de construção” in the “Desenhar” group. New lines, those typed by measure too, are then construction lines. The button switches back to normal lines. A line you have drawn already becomes a construction line when you click it and choose “Construção”. “Transformar em linha” makes it a normal line again. New points snap to where a construction line crosses another line, a blue ring shows it, and to the ends of the construction line. That is how you put a corner on a middle, at a fixed distance from an edge or on a crossing, without calculating. New points also snap to the middle of every straight line of the sketch, to the centre of every circle and rounded corner, and to the middles of the sides of a body shown underneath (#624). A point that is being dragged ignores the middle of its own lines. “Linha a partir do meio” in the “Desenhar” group draws a line from its middle: click the middle first, then the end, and the line runs the same length to the other side. The middle becomes a point of its own. Click the button again to draw normal lines. A construction line does not cut the outline apart where it crosses it. When revolving it may lie to the right of the axis too.

Click “Concluir esboço”. The outline stands as a body on the workplane. In its settings you change the height, the colour and everything else as with any other shape. When you resize it, PrintCaddy builds it again from the sketch a moment later, and the sketch grows with it. So it stays an exact body that takes chamfers and fillets, and the next time you edit it the sketch has the size the body has. If the workplane lies on the side of a body, you draw the way you look at that side: up in the sketch is up on the finished body too. The faint outline of the body in the sketch view shows where it stands. If the workplane cuts through a body, the sketch view shows the outline of that cut instead, so a hollow body appears as a ring and you can line the sketch up with its walls. A point you set or drag close to a corner of these outlines snaps exactly onto it; a small blue ring shows it. That way you take edges of other bodies into the sketch, even when the workplane does not lie exactly on them. To trace round existing work, switch on “Mostrar no plano do esboço todas as arestas das peças ao fundo” (the layers button in the view buttons on the left): all the edges of the bodies are then drawn on the sketch plane, thin and faint, as if you looked through them, whatever height they lie at. A plane that stands upright, set on a front face for example, shows the front view this way. The choice is kept in the browser. The outline has become a body. The corner is rounded. With “Editar esboço” you can return to the sketch at any time to change it. A double click on the body does the same, as in Tinkercad (a locked body stays closed); “Clique duplo abre o esboço” in the settings switches that off. Edge treatments you already made on the body are lost, though, because the edges are created anew. A body you turned or moved in the 3D editor opens where it stands on the plate, turned as you see it there and on the plate's grid; only a tilted or mirrored body opens in its own frame. A sketch with several outlines makes one body, and outlines that overlap merge in it. To have every outline on its own, select the body and click “Separar peças”: each outer outline becomes a body of its own, with the holes that lie in it, and keeps the body's height, colour and place. Each part has its own sketch to edit, with the construction lines, so you can raise or lower the parts one by one and join or cut them afterwards. Edge treatments block this, as does a body stretched since: it is then taken apart as a mesh. Another kind of body from the same sketch: the badge at the top of the sketch says what it becomes, “Esboço de extrusão”, “Esboço de revolução” or “Esboço de varredura”. Click it and pick another, also while you edit an existing body: an imported SVG, which comes in extruded, becomes a vase or a knob when you switch it to “Esboço de revolução”. An outline reaching across the axis moves left until its right edge lies on the axis, so the half cross-section of an SVG turns about its straight side; Ctrl+Z takes the move back. When you finish, the new body takes the old one's place, name and colour, its foot at the same height. Edge treatments go, as with every edit of a sketch.

When revolving, you draw half the cross-section to the left of the axis shown in the sketch. Next to it you see a 3D preview of the revolve. It shows at once what the body will look like. You can turn, shift and zoom it with the mouse; the small button in its top right corner, or a double click on it, brings back the first view. The outline must be closed, or you build an open line as a stroke, see below. At the end click “Concluir revolução”. The other bodies of the design are shown from the front, in the same view as the profile, with the axis standing at the middle: draw the profile next to them or above them. The body stands where you drew it, and the horizontal line through the middle of the sketch is the ground: a profile drawn above it gives a body that stands higher, and its lowest point is the foot of the body. A revolved body is an exact body, like an extruded one: it takes chamfers and fillets, and you can hollow it, for a cup or a vase. A body revolved with an older PrintCaddy is a mesh; open “Editar esboço” and finish it again to make it exact. A profile that reaches across the axis cannot be built exactly and becomes a mesh, as before. One continuous strand: “Passo”. A revolve turns its outline into closed rings. Select the revolved body and give it a “Passo” above 0 in the Properties panel, the distance it climbs per turn, and the outline winds up as a helix instead: one continuous strand, like filament on a spool or a coil. “Abertura” then becomes “Voltas”, up to 200; a negative number winds left-handed. Turns closer than the outline is high melt into one body, so a solid core with a fine pitch works too. A helix is built as a mesh, so fillet, chamfer and hollow do not work on it; keep “Lados” low on many turns. A pitch of 0 makes rings again.

“Varredura do esboço” pulls an outline along a path: a cable channel that turns a corner, a conduit, a guard round a belt, a ring around a hexagon. It sits next to “Extrusão do esboço” and “Revolução do esboço” in the “Criar” group. You draw two things on the same sheet: The cross-section as a closed outline, as usual. Draw it as you would see it looking along the path from its start: across the path is the sketch's left and right, up is up on the finished body. A hollow section, a channel or a tube, is an outline with another one inside it. By default the section is centred on the path. The menu next to the mode badge at the top lets you put its left or right edge on the path instead (“No caminho: borda esquerda”, “No caminho: borda direita”, seen looking along the path), so a rail can sit on one side of the line or follow the edge of a part. The body stands on the sketch plane with the lowest point of the section. The path as a “Linha de construção”: switch it on and draw lines or curves, one chain, open or closed (a closed chain gives a ring). The path lies flat in the sketch plane. Draw the section near the end of the path where it should start; the path starts at the end nearest to it. Then click “Concluir varredura”. A corner of straight pieces becomes a mitre, a curve stays smooth, and the section stays upright all the way. The body is exact, like an extruded one: fillet, chamfer and the STEP export work on it. If a closed outline or a path is missing, or there are several separate paths, PrintCaddy says so. With “Editar esboço” you can return to the sketch and change the section or the path.

Normally the area inside a closed outline becomes the body. With “Traço” in the “Concluir” section you build the line itself instead, with a width you set. Tick “Construir como traço” in the panel; the sketch shows straight away what comes out. A closed outline becomes a frame. “Posição” says where the wall lies: “Centralizado” on the drawn line, “Interno” within it or “Externo” outside it. Outside is handy for a tolerance: draw the outline of a hole, a dovetail for instance, and give it a 0.2 mm stroke outside to get the gap the print needs. An open line becomes a stripe, centred on the line. “Pontas” sets how its ends look: “Retas”, “Quadradas” (longer by half the width) or “Redondas”. “Cantos” applies to both: “Vivos”, “Redondos” or “Chanfrados”. The sketch keeps the drawn line. Open it again and you go on changing line and stroke; untick the box and the area is built again. Curves are broken into short straight pieces for it. In a revolve the stroke is a thin wall: draw the wall of a vase or a cup as one open line to the left of the axis, tick “Traço” and set the width, and the revolve turns that band. What reaches across the axis is cut off at it.

You can set the stroke without opening the sketch too: in the properties of a sketch body, choose “Área”, “Traço externo”, “Traço interno” or “Traço centralizado” under “Preenchimento”, with “Largura da linha” and “Cantos”. The body is built again straight away, where it stands. These match the fill modes of Tinkercad's SVG import: default, outer line and inner line. “Mais largo” keeps the area filled and grows it by the line width all round, with sharp, round or bevelled corners: a base layer under a logo for a multicolour print, which the stroke outside alone would only give as a ring. “Mais estreito” does the opposite: the area stays filled and its edge moves in by the line width all round, holes included (they grow). Use both on copies of one sketch for a fit: the hole at its drawn size, the part that goes through it “Mais estreito” by 0.5 mm, or a wall inside a shape cut from the same outline. A width larger than the outline allows leaves nothing. In the sketch's stroke panel the same two choices stand under “Posição”. With a line outside, inside or centred, “Cutting Edge” makes the wall sharp on top: its top runs in to that width with a 45° chamfer on both sides, as on a cookie cutter. 0 leaves the top flat; the edge stays when you change the line width. “Silhueta (sem furos)” leaves out every outline lying inside another: holes and whatever lies in them. Only the outer outline stays. Together with “Traço externo” it makes a cookie cutter: import an SVG twice, once with the silhouette as an area for the base and once with the silhouette and 1 to 2 mm of stroke outside as the wall. The switch is in the “Traço” panel in sketch mode as well. Fillets and chamfers on the edges go when the body is built again, as when the sketch is edited.

An extruded sketch has vertical walls. A stamp, an embossing die or a punch wants slanted ones, outside and inside, with the same wall thickness all the way. PrintCaddy has no draft angle for an extrusion, but for plain outlines the “Afunilamento” gets you there. One way that works: Draw the outline with the hole it needs and make a body of it. Duplicate the body (Ctrl+D). On the first body, switch on “Silhueta (sem furos)”, so the hole is filled, and give it a wider bottom than top with “Afunilamento”. On the copy, open its sketch again and delete the outer outline, so that only the outline of the hole is left. Finish the sketch, switch the body to “Orifício” and give it a narrower bottom than top with “Afunilamento”. Move the hole into the first body, where the hole was, and group the two. The walls now slope outside and inside. Taper scales the whole outline, so this is exact for plain shapes, where you can choose the sizes so the walls run parallel, and only an approximation for fine details such as lettering.

With “Adicionar imagem” you put a photo or a drawing under the sketch and trace it, at any time, also before the first line. You can set its size, opacity and position. Once the picture sits right, lock it with Ctrl+L so you do not move it by accident while drawing. A locked image is out of the way: clicks go through it, so you can pick lines and points on top of it and drag a frame over them. The padlock in its corner unlocks it with one click; Alt+click selects it without unlocking it. If its settings at the right edge cover the picture, drag them away by their title bar; a double-click on it docks them again. Under “Alinhar” you line up a photo that was not taken straight: “Rotação”: Turn the picture about its centre, with the curved arrows beyond its corners or as a number in degrees. With Shift the arrows snap in 15° steps. Inside the ring that appears while turning they snap to 22.5°, outside it to whole degrees. “Para X = 0” and “Para Y = 0”: put the picture's centre on X = 0 or Y = 0. For a revolve, X = 0 is the axis, so the picture then lies symmetric about it. “Calibrar”: Its button sits at the top, right under the preview. Click two points in the picture whose distance you know, the ends of a ruler or a known diameter, and type the real distance. The picture is scaled evenly so that distance is right; the first point stays where it was. “Recortar”: The handles on the frame now crop the picture instead of scaling it; what is cut away stays stored and comes back with “Mostrar imagem inteira” or when a handle is pulled out again. All four touch the reference only, never the sketch.

Key Effect Esc put the note tool down; otherwise put the tool down (back to “Selecionar”), then clear the selection Delete delete the selected element Ctrl+C copy the selection Ctrl+X cut the selection Ctrl+V paste Ctrl+D duplicate the selection Ctrl+Z undo Ctrl+A select every point and line Ctrl+I “Adicionar imagem” Shift while drawing: snap the line in 15° steps; while dragging: keep movement on one axis digit, <, Tab, Enter while drawing: type and set the length and angle of the next line R rotate the closed sketch by 45° Ctrl+L lock or unlock the selected outline, or the template image N place a note: the next click puts it on the sketch Shift+N show or hide the notes Tip: Draw as few points as needed. An outline with a few well-placed points gives a smoother body than a tangle of many.
Raised or engraved lettering in eight typefaces or one of your own, and if you like along a circular arc, such as on a coin, a lid or a ring.

Choose “Texto” in the shape library and place it. In the “Texto” field on the right, type what it should say. The settings below: “Fonte”: Eight typefaces are available: Multilanguage, Sans, Serif, Script, Monospace, Rounded, Stencil (letters made of straight lines) and Japanese (Zen Maru Gothic). New text starts in Sans. Accented letters such as ä, ö, ü, é and the € sign are in every typeface, and so are kana, the common kanji and many of the rare ones in names such as 澤, 槇 and 檜: a Japanese name works in every typeface and on a name tag. The Japanese letters are fetched the first time a text needs them (the rare kanji in a second file, only when a text has one), so such a text shows question marks for a moment. They are kept on the computer afterwards, so Japanese also works offline from then on. Fonts of your own come on top, see Your own fonts below. “Tamanho das letras”: How big the letters are, seen from above; “Altura” sets how thick they are. “Altura”: How far the lettering stands out from the surface. “Bisel”: Rounds the letter edges so they look softer. With “Segmentos” you decide in how many steps. “Borda das letras”: rounds or chamfers the top edge of the letters, as on a name tag: “Nenhuma”, “Arredondada” or “Chanfrada”, with the “Tamanho da borda” (0.4 mm to start with, at most as high as the text). It goes further than the “Bisel”, but only as far as the strokes are wide: where a stroke is thinner than twice the size, the edge ends in a narrower top. The underside stays flat, so single letters can be glued on afterwards. While an edge is chosen it takes the place of “Bisel”. Size: You set the length and width of the line as with any shape. Drag the handles or type the dimensions. “Espaçamento entre letras (%)”: The space between the letters on top of the one the font has, in per cent of the letter size: 0 leaves it as the font made it, above it the letters stand further apart, below it (down to -50) tighter, which a font of your own often needs. The letters keep their size and the box follows the line, on straight and on curved text. The spacing is not applied to Arabic and Hebrew, whose letters join up. “Esticar as letras até a moldura”: Off at first: the letters keep their proportions and sit in the middle of the frame, so a frame pulled wider or deeper than the word needs stays larger than the letters. Switch it on and the letters are stretched to fill the whole frame in both directions: a capital can be made lower or narrower, as in Tinkercad. It is for straight text; curved text has its own letter size. “Letras de cima para baixo”: Stacks the letters top to bottom, each in the middle of one upright line, for a sign on a door frame or a name down a pen. The box turns upright and the letters keep their size; “Espaçamento entre letras (%)” sets the gap between them. Curved text has no such switch. Text is at first a single body. If you want to treat the letters individually, click “Separar peças”. Then every letter is a shape of its own. The edges of text can be chamfered or filleted too, straight or curved, see Breaking edges and hollowing bodies. Use small sizes such as 0.2 to 0.5 mm, because the strokes of the letters are narrow.

The list under “Fonte” draws every font in its own letters, with the words of your text, so you see how they will look before you choose. The same goes for the fonts in the window below; the fonts listed from your computer show their names in their own letters. Arrow keys and Enter work in the list, and a letter jumps to the next font that starts with it. Besides the eight built-in fonts you can use any font of your own: a font file from your computer or, in Chrome and Edge, a font installed on your computer. Choose “Suas próprias fontes …” at the bottom of “Fonte”.
