The “Suas próprias fontes” window opens. “Escolher um arquivo de fonte …” takes a TrueType file (.ttf), an OpenType file (.otf) or a WOFF file (.woff). You can also simply drag the file into the window. On Windows the installed fonts live in the Fonts folder (C:\Windows\Fonts). The browser's file dialog hides it. Open it in Explorer instead and drag the font into the “Suas próprias fontes” window. Fonts installed for you alone live in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Fonts, which the file dialog shows too. On a Mac fonts live in /Library/Fonts and ~/Library/Fonts. “Fonte do computador …” lists the fonts installed on your computer. The first time, the browser asks whether PrintCaddy may read them. The search field finds a font quickly, a click takes it. If a text is selected, it gets the new font at once. Otherwise the font shows up under “Fonte” in the “Suas próprias fontes” group, and “Usar” in the window puts it on the selected texts. Fonts of your own work like the built-in ones: text on a circular arc, chamfers and fillets on the edges and the STEP export all work the same. Letters a font lacks are taken from Sans.

Arabic, Persian, Urdu and Hebrew are written right to left: the first letter stands on the right, and in a mixed text such as "Name عربي" only the Arabic word runs backwards, digits stay as usual. Arabic letters join their neighbours the way the script asks, and lam-alef becomes a ligature. This needs a font that has these letters; the built-in ones do not. Add one of your own, such as Arial, Tahoma or Segoe UI on Windows, or a free one such as Noto Naskh Arabic, Noto Sans Arabic or Amiri. Vowel marks sit on the letter they belong to. Text on a circular arc, outline, silhouette, layers and name tags work with it as with any other text.

Browser Choose a font file Font from the computer Chrome and Edge on a computer, the installed PrintCaddy app too yes yes, after the browser asks Firefox yes no Safari on a Mac yes no Tablet and phone yes, from the device's files no Web pages may not simply read the installed fonts. Only Chrome and Edge have a permission for it, and only on secure pages, over https as on the public site. When PrintCaddy runs over http, say on your own server or as a Docker install in your home network, “Fonte do computador …” is missing; drag the font over from Explorer then. In the other browsers you choose the font file from the fonts folder, with the same result. If you declined the question in Chrome or Edge, allow it again in the site settings, behind the padlock to the left of the address. PrintCaddy cannot read WOFF2 files (there is almost always a TTF or OTF version), font collections (.ttc, several fonts in one file) or colour emoji fonts. From very large fonts, such as Chinese ones, PrintCaddy takes the first 8000 characters. A variable font is read in its default setting, usually the regular weight. Some fonts, script and variable fonts above all, draw a letter from strokes that overlap. PrintCaddy merges them into one clean outline when it reads the font, so the body stays printable. Such letters are then made of very short straight pieces instead of curves; it does not show.

A font of your own stays in this browser on this computer. Another browser or another computer does not know it until you add it there too. Clearing the browser's site data clears the fonts as well. In the “Suas próprias fontes” window the bin removes a font from the browser. Your designs lose nothing by it, as the next section shows.

h: Passing on designs with a font of your own
t: A design does not store the font file, only the outlines of the letters its texts use, those in earlier steps of the history included. If a text says "Hello", only H, e, l and o travel with it. That holds for every way a design is saved: in the browser, on your own server, as a .lyl file and in “Formas personalizadas”. So: The design opens correctly anywhere, also on a computer without the font. The texts look the same and can be moved, turned, scaled and filleted. New letters need the font. If someone without the font types a letter the design did not bring along, PrintCaddy draws it from Sans. Under “Fonte” the font is then marked “só as letras do projeto”. Adding the font file brings back every letter. Exports hold geometry only. STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP and SVG contain bodies and outlines, no font. Older PrintCaddy versions do not know fonts of one's own yet and draw such texts in Multilanguage. Licences: Fonts are protected by copyright, and their licence says what you may do with them. The embedded letter outlines are what PDF files take along from a font, and most licences allow that. Some commercial fonts, though, forbid passing on even single letters. Before you pass on or publish a design with a font of your own, check the font's licence. Free fonts such as those from Google Fonts (mostly under the SIL Open Font License) can be passed on without worry. For a printed part or an exported STL it does not matter: they hold no font any more, only geometry.

Raised: Place the text on the surface and group it with the body. It grows out as a relief. Engraved: Switch the text to “Orifício”, let it reach a little into the surface and group it with the body. The letters are then engraved. For lettering on a side face, first put the workplane on that face, see View and workplane.

A text need not be built as filled letters. “Preenchimento” in the properties offers the same choice as Tinkercad: “Preenchido”: the letters as they are. “Contorno”: a line along the outline of the letters, half inside and half outside it. “Linha externa”: a line round the outside of the letters. “Linha interna”: a line on the inside of the letters. With a line chosen, two settings appear right under the list: “Largura da linha” sets how thick the line is, “Cantos” how it goes round the corners (“Redondos”, “Chanfrados” or “Vivos”). The rarer settings are under “Mais”: “Silhueta (sem furos)” leaves out the holes in O, A or e, and “Mais largo (base para impressão multicolorida)” keeps the letters filled and makes them thicker by the line width all round; letters that touch grow into one piece. With a line outside, a centred line or "Wider" the box of the text grows, while the letters keep their size. “Bisel” and “Segmentos” exist for filled letters only.

A name tag for a multicolour print is a text in layers: the letters on top, under them the same text a little wider in a second colour, at the bottom a plate without holes in a third. PrintCaddy makes it in one click: A new name tag: choose “Etiqueta de nome” in the shape library and place it. It says "Name" in white letters on a red rim and a dark plate. From a text: select the text and click “Criar camadas” at the top of its settings. All settings of the tag are in the card “Etiqueta de nome”, at the top of the settings: “Texto” and “Fonte”, fonts of your own too. The tag grows with the words. “Tamanho das letras”: how tall the capital letters are, in mm. All layers follow and stay lined up. “Letras de cima para baixo”: stands the tag upright with the letters under one another, all layers along. “Camadas”: one row per layer, from the top down. Each row has the colour (click the coloured square), how much wider the layer is than the letters, its height and “Sem furos”, which fills the holes in letters such as O and A. “Cantos” sets how a wider layer goes round the corners of the letters: “Redondos”, “Chanfrados” or “Vivos”. The top row is the letters themselves. + adds a layer at the bottom, – takes the bottom layer away. A tag has two to six layers. “Furo para chaveiro”: gives the bottom layer a straight tab with a round end and a hole for a key ring; the tab grows with the hole. A 3 mm hole, the default, makes a tab 6.5 mm wide that sticks out 6.75 mm, the hole's edge 2 mm from the edge of the bottom layer. Choose the “Diâmetro do furo” and the “Lado”: “Esquerda”, “Direita” or “Em cima”. “Livre” takes the hole off the tag and puts a “Aba para chaveiro” of its own beside it, in the bottom layer's colour and height: an ordinary shape you move and turn with its handles wherever the tag needs it. Once it is in place, “Fixar na etiqueta” in its panel makes it part of the nearest tag, just where it is: the hole goes through every layer it reaches, the ear joins the bottom layer, and both keep to that corner of the letters when the words or the size change. “Livre” brings the tab out again where it was, to move it once more. The hole goes through every layer it touches, and the tab moves along when you change the words, the letter size or the font. “Posição ao longo do lado” moves the tab up or down along its side (along the top: left or right), up to where it would leave the side; 0 is the middle. Use it when the middle of the side meets a gap, as beside a J, and move the tab to the part of the letter that reaches out. “Borda das letras”: rounds or chamfers the top edge of the letters on the top layer, the way a printed tag is finished: “Nenhuma”, “Arredondada” or “Chanfrada”, with the “Tamanho da borda” (0.4 mm to start with, at most as high as the layer). It works for every font and word. The edge is part of the letters' mesh, so the edge tool takes such a text as a mesh, which for a text this fine is heavy; pick the edge here instead. Every change shows at once. The tag is a bundle: it moves as one, and each layer stays a body of its own in its own colour, the way a slicer needs them for a multicolour print. To round or bevel the edges of one layer, click “Editar conjunto” and pick the layer, see Breaking edges and hollowing bodies.

Type the names into “Lista de nomes”, one per line, up to a hundred. The button below says how many tags it will make, for example "Make 12 name tags". Every tag gets the same layers, letter size and key ring hole and is an object of its own; they are laid out in rows below the first, 5 mm apart. A plain text has the name list too, further down in its settings.

An icon tag is the same tag with an SVG icon instead of letters: a heart, a cloud, a club's logo. The icon on top, under it the same outline a little wider in a second colour, at the bottom a plate without holes. A new icon tag: choose “Etiqueta de ícone” in the shape library. A small window opens: click “Procurar…”, pick an SVG, PNG or JPG file, check the picture, type the “Largura (mm)” of the icon and click “OK”. The tag stands in the middle of the plate, in the same layers as a new name tag. From a sketch body: an imported SVG, or a sketch you drew, has “Criar camadas” at the top of its settings. The card “Etiqueta de ícone” at the top of the settings holds: “Outro arquivo…”: puts the icon of another file (SVG, PNG or JPG) on the tag; the layers and the width stay as they are. “Largura”: how wide the icon on top is, in mm. All layers follow and stay lined up. “Camadas”: the rows as on a name tag - colour, how much wider, “Cantos”, height and “Sem furos”, + and –, two to six layers. The top row is the icon itself. “Furo para chaveiro”: as on a name tag: a hole for a key ring through every layer, with a tab with a round end on the bottom layer, beyond the icon. “Diâmetro do furo” and “Lado” choose its size and where it sits; “Livre” gives a tab of its own, as on a name tag. The tab is made for the outline of the icon, so on a very ragged icon check where it meets the plate. “Posição ao longo do lado” moves the tab along its side, as on the name tag. “Quantidade”: how many tags you want, 1 to 100. “Quantas couberem” works it out from the plate of the printer chosen in the settings, for small logos a full plate. The button below makes them, 5 mm apart, laid out on the middle of the plate; the first is the tag itself. The SVG needs closed outlines; a drawing of open lines only cannot become a tag. A sketch body whose fill is a line keeps it: the area of that line is the icon. A picture (PNG or JPG) is traced into an outline, and the preview shows the outline. Under “Contornado a partir de” you choose whether the “Parte escura” or the “Parte clara” becomes the icon; at first it is the part that is not the background. Transparent pixels never belong to the icon. An SVG that holds nothing but one picture, as Inkscape saves an imported bitmap, is traced the same way. The outline follows the pixels, so a small picture gives a rough edge: pictures of a few hundred pixels or more work best. “Outro arquivo…” takes the part of a picture that is not its background.

A QR code turns a text or a web address into a pattern a phone camera reads: a link to your shop on a sign, the Wi-Fi name on a coaster, a phone number on a key tag. Choose “QR code” in the shape library. A window opens; the cursor is already in the text field: “Texto ou endereço”: what the code says. Enter makes the code, Shift+Enter starts a new line. Below the field you see how much of the room is used; umlauts and other special letters take two bytes. When the text is too long, the field says so. “Correção de erros”: L, M, Q or H. A higher level can still be read when part of the code is dirty or scratched (L about 7 %, M 15 %, Q 25 %, H 30 %), but needs more modules for the same text, so each module gets smaller. M is chosen at first. “Construir como”: “Só o código” makes the code alone, 4 mm high. “Em relevo sobre uma placa” puts it 1 mm high on a white plate 3 mm thick, as a bundle of two colours, so a multicolour print prints the code dark and the plate light. “Gravado” cuts the code 1 mm deep into the plate. “Tamanho por”: type the “Largura” of the whole code (40 mm at first) or the size of one module; the other number is shown below. Modules under 0.8 mm get a warning. That is a rule of thumb for a 0.4 mm nozzle, not a guarantee: printer, material, colours and the phone all play a part. “Zona de silêncio (4 módulos)”: scanners need an empty rim four modules wide round the code. On a plate the rim is part of the plate; switch it off only if the plate sits on a larger light surface. The code alone has no rim of its own: leave the room free round it. Heights: the height of the code, or on a plate the code height or engraving depth, and the plate thickness. The preview shows the code as it will be built. “OK” puts it in the middle of the plate. The code is a body like any other: move it, turn it, scale it (keep width and depth the same, or the code is stretched), group it, or make it a hole and group it into a part of your own to engrave it there. Scaling it scales the whole code; each module stays square. The card “QR code” at the top of its settings holds the text. Change it and click “Criar de novo”: the code is built again where it stands and as wide as it is now. Error correction, quiet zone and build stay as they were chosen; for other choices make a new code from the library. Scan the code with your phone before you print it, and once more after printing. Dark on light reads best; a light code on a dark plate is not read by every phone.

Should the lettering not run straight but follow the edge of a coin, a lid or a ring? For that there is the setting “Em arco”. Text follows a circle. All letters stand on one common line. Once you switch it on, the text runs along the circle. All letters stand on the same baseline, as evenly as with normal text. There are four settings: “Raio do arco” (5 to 500 mm): The radius of the circle the letters' baseline runs on. “Tamanho das letras”: How tall the letters are. It no longer depends on the width of the shape. “Pela parte de baixo”: Moves the text from the top of the circle to its bottom. The letters then point with their heads to the centre. “De cabeça para baixo”: Turns only the letters over so you can read them from the other side. The text stays in its place on the circle. The centre of the circle is the centre of the shape. That is why aligning works as usual: if you centre the text with a cylinder or ring, it sits exactly concentric on it. When you pull a handle, radius and letter size grow together, so the lettering is not distorted. Tip: At the top of the circle the letters stand outside the baseline; with “Pela parte de baixo” they stand inside, heads towards the centre. For the lettering to fit on a disc, the radius plus the letter size should be smaller than the disc's radius.

Screws, nuts and tapped holes that fit together, plus gear, spring, bent tube, dovetail, teardrop hole, counterbore and countersink. Besides the basic shapes, the library contains some parts that would be tedious to put together yourself. All of them can be changed afterwards in their settings.

Choose “Rosca” in the shape library. Under “Tipo” you decide what it should be: “Barra roscada”: a cylinder with thread, for example a screw without a head. “Parafuso”: with a head. You choose the “Cabeça”: “Cabeça cilíndrica (Allen)”, “Cabeça escareada” or “Cabeça sextavada”. “Porca”: the matching nut. “Furo roscado”: a tapped hole. It is a hole. Drag it into a part, group both, and the part has an internal thread. A screw with a cylinder head. On the right: kind and head shape, further down size, pitch and profile. You pick the size under “Tamanho” from a list: metric from M2 to M24, the inch sizes UNC and UNF from No. 4 to 1 inch, and the pipe threads G1/16 to G4. If you choose “Personalizado”, you set “Diâmetro” and “Passo” yourself. For an inch size or a G size the field asks for “Fios por polegada” instead of the pitch in millimetres. The list groups the sizes by series, and a line under the field names the series of the size you picked, with examples you know from everyday life: M, metric coarse: the ISO metric coarse thread to ISO 261, as on standard screws and nuts. UNC, US inch coarse: the camera and tripod screw is 1/4"-20 UNC (ISO 1222), larger tripod heads use 3/8"-16 UNC. UNF, US inch fine: the same diameters as UNC with a finer pitch (ASME B1.1). G, pipe thread: a shower hose connects with G1/2, a washing-machine inlet hose with G3/4. A garden tap ends in G3/4, smaller taps in G1/2; that is where the tap connector of a click-on hose system screws on. The G sizes are the parallel Whitworth pipe threads to ISO 228-1, found on fittings for water, gas, hydraulics and pneumatics. The size names the pipe, not the thread: a G1 measures 33.249 mm across the thread. Choosing a G size sets the profile to “Whitworth (55°)”, and choosing a metric or inch size sets it back to “Triangular (ISO)”. A “Trapezoidal” or “Redonda” profile you picked yourself stays. The standard only defines the thread, so the head of a screw and a nut on a G size get the same proportions as on a diameter you set yourself. The tapered pipe threads R, Rc and Rp are not included. More settings: “Sentido”: “Rosca direita” or “Rosca esquerda”. “Perfil”: “Triangular (ISO)” is the standard profile of metric and inch threads, “Whitworth (55°)” that of the G pipe threads: 55° with rounded crests and roots. “Trapezoidal” and “Redonda” have flat crests and roots. That usually prints more reliably because no thin tips result. “Personalizada (trapézio)”: A trapezoid you shape yourself, with a flat crest and a flat root of the same width. “Ângulo do flanco” is the angle between the two flanks of a tooth: 60° is the sharp V thread, 30° the trapezoid thread, and at 90° or less no flank is flatter than 45°, so the thread prints without supports. “Profundidade da rosca” and “Diâmetro do núcleo” are one measure said two ways: the core diameter is the diameter minus twice the depth, and changing one changes the other. A new own profile starts with the V thread's depth at 60°. The depth has limits that depend on the angle and the pitch: not shallower than a tenth of the pitch, not deeper than 40 % of the diameter, and not so deep that the two flanks take more than nine tenths of the pitch. If you change the pitch, the depth follows in proportion; if you scale the thread, so does the depth. The play and the chamfers work as with the other profiles. Through the MCP bridge the profile is custom with threadFlankAngle and threadDepth. “Folga (XY)”: For nut and tapped hole, the room that makes sure a printed pair really turns. The coarser your printer works, the more clearance the pair needs. It is the extra room across the whole diameter, and the gap between the flanks of a V thread is only about half of it, so a printed pair needs more than you might expect: new nuts start at 0.4 mm, 0.3 is tight and 0.5 loose. Print a test pair first. Rods and screws have a clearance of their own here, which makes the bolt that much thinner in diameter. It is set to 0. Which side gets the room depends on what you pair: Printed screw and printed nut: leave the screw at 0 and give the nut the room (the 0.4 mm it starts with). Real screw in a printed nut or tapped hole: the printed side takes all of it, so the nut keeps its 0.4 mm. A tighter 0.3 mm is worth a test if the screw wobbles. Printed screw in a real nut: the real nut has no play, so the screw has to be thinner: 0.3 to 0.4 mm here, as much as a printed nut would have. “Folga ao longo do eixo (Z)”: For nut and tapped hole, the play along the axis, on top of the “Folga (XY)”. Every tooth of the nut gets this much thinner, the diameter stays as it is. The reason: the “Folga (XY)” works on the diameter only and opens the flanks of a V thread to about 0.58 of its value. Anyone who wants air between the flanks has to open the diameter wide and gets sideways slop for it. The play along the axis sets the two apart. It is set to 0, so a saved thread does not change, and it goes up to a fifth of the pitch at most, because above that nothing would be left of the nut's teeth. The field exists for nut and tapped hole only; rod and screw keep their own clearance. More below under "Threads for 3D printing". “Chanfro, ponta superior”, “Chanfro, ponta inferior”, “Chanfro da cabeça” and “Chanfro da borda”: Chamfers at the ends so the thread starts cleanly and the head has no sharp edge. Each end of a rod, nut or tapped hole has its own chamfer, so the top can be long and the bottom short or none. A screw has only one at its tip, labelled “Chanfro”. On a nut or tapped hole the chamfer is the room the mouth opens beyond the outer diameter; the cone runs at 45 degrees on down to the thread core, so no ledge is left at the outer diameter. Switching a thread between “Barra roscada” and “Furo roscado” keeps its length. A nut and a screw start from their standard measures. “Qualidade”: How finely the thread is calculated. Higher is more exact, but slower. Printed threads are a topic of their own. Make the screw-and-nut pair as a test first before you print a large part, and adjust the clearance to your printer.

A printed thread needs air in two places, and they act differently: Clearance in the diameter (“Folga (XY)”): makes the nut wider. The screw then has half the value as air on each side, 0.2 mm at 0.4 mm. The thread turns easily, but the screw can wobble sideways. Play along the axis (“Folga ao longo do eixo (Z)”): makes the teeth of the nut thinner. The screw can then move back and forth along the axis by that value when it is not tightened. There is no extra air to the side for it. Together they make the gap between the flanks: about 0.58 times the clearance in the diameter plus the play along the axis. An example for a 0.3 mm gap: it used to take 0.5 mm in the diameter, that is 0.25 mm of air on each side. Now 0.2 mm in the diameter (0.1 mm on each side) and 0.2 mm along the axis do it, and the gap is 0.32 mm. Consequences to know The screw has play along the axis. Without load it can move back and forth by that value. For fastenings, lids and housings that does not matter; for a lead screw that has to position exactly it does, so keep it small or at 0 there. The nut's teeth get thinner. With 0.3 mm at a pitch of 1.75 mm every tooth is almost a third thinner at its middle and so clearly less strong. For heavily loaded parts take a coarser thread instead. More to calculate. The tooth shape gets extra points, so the thread has more triangles and takes a little longer to compute. No true arc in the STEP export for the Whitworth profile. A “Whitworth (55°)” thread with play along the axis goes to the edge tool and the STEP export as a tooth shape made of straight pieces, not with the true circular arcs. At 0 everything stays as before. Tips A test pair first. A screw and a nut, each only 4 to 6 mm tall, take a few minutes. Print three pairs with different play side by side and take the one that turns easily and does not wobble. Start with values that often fit. Clearance in the diameter 0.2 to 0.3 mm and play along the axis 0.2 mm. If the screw wobbles sideways, lower the clearance in the diameter; if it jams, raise the play along the axis. If you would rather do without the play along the axis, use 0.4 mm in the diameter as before. The play along the axis should be at least one layer height. What lies below one layer the printer does not resolve. With a layer height of 0.2 mm, 0.2 mm is a good start; with 0.1 mm, less is enough. Print screw and nut upright. The axis points up, so every turn lies in whole layers and the flanks come out clean. Lying down, the flanks sag. Fine pitches are hard. Below about 1 mm of pitch the turns often fuse. A coarser thread, or a “Trapezoidal” profile with flat crests, prints more reliably than a fine V thread. Avoid thin tips. The V thread has a narrow tip that the printer hardly hits with its nozzle width. The “Trapezoidal” and “Redonda” profiles have flatter teeth. Deburr and run it in. The first turns are often stiff because small remains of the print stand on the flanks. Turn it back and forth a few times and it runs easier. The chamfer at the start helps threading it in. Another printer or filament. The play depends on the printer, the material and the nozzle. Print the test pair again when you change either. The edge tool takes a thread as its exact body. You can chamfer or round the part that carries it with the thread already in place, or the rims of a screw head, see Breaking edges and hollowing bodies. Working out a thread's edges takes a while: a few seconds for an M6, about half a minute for a G1/2 pipe thread. The quickest way to break the edge of a screw head is still the head chamfer in the properties.

“Engrenagem” comes as “Engrenagem reta”, “Engrenagem helicoidal”, “Engrenagem espinha de peixe” and “Engrenagem cônica”, and as “Coroa interna” and “Cremalheira” (further down). New gears have “Evolvente” under “Forma do dente”: teeth with involute flanks, as gear generators and engineering use them. Such teeth roll cleanly on each other. You set the number of “Dentes” (6 to 500) and the “Módulo (mm)”, and the size follows: the outside diameter is module × (teeth + 2), the pitch circle module × teeth. New gears start at module 2. Two gears mesh when they have the same module and the same “Ângulo de pressão” (usually 20°) and their centres stand (teeth + teeth) × module / 2 apart. Select both gears and the properties panel gives that centre distance and how far apart the centres are now. If the gears should stay where they are, it also names the module at which they would mesh there, and “Ajustar o módulo das duas” gives both gears that module in one step; each keeps its teeth, height and centre hole. If a tooth then meets a tooth instead of a gap, turn one of the gears by half a tooth, which is 180° divided by its number of teeth. “Folga entre dentes” takes a little off the teeth so a printed pair does not bind. The value is for the pair, and each gear takes half of it; 0.2 mm is a good start, 0 gives the exact gear. Below the base circle the flank runs straight down to the root and is not undercut as a cutter would do it. That suits printing, but a very small pinion below about 17 teeth may rub slightly at the root. A helical gear adds the “Ângulo da hélice”. With involute teeth it is the true helix angle on the pitch circle: two helical gears mesh when they have the same module and the same angle, one positive and the other negative. The “Engrenagem espinha de peixe” is two helical halves turning opposite ways: the teeth run one way up to half the height and back after it, like an arrow. That has two advantages for 3D printing: the gear centres itself on its shaft, and it has no axial thrust, because the forces of the two halves cancel. A helical gear, in contrast, pushes sideways along its axis. You set the “Ângulo da hélice” and the “Qualidade da hélice” as for the helical gear; the angle applies to each half. Two herringbone gears mesh when they have the same module and the same angle with opposite signs, one positive and the other negative. There is no groove in the middle, as on milled herringbone gears: the two halves run into each other without a step. The edge tool and the STEP export take the herringbone gear as a triangle mesh, not as an exact body. The bevel gear takes the involute teeth and makes them smaller towards its top. That is an approximation, not an exactly worked out bevel pair. “Redondo” are round teeth made of arcs, like Tinkercad's Useful gear: tip and gap run into each other without a corner. Small gears print more forgivingly that way and turn more easily, and on a knob the teeth make a pleasant grip. Round teeth are set by “Dentes”, “Módulo (mm)” and “Folga entre dentes” too; they have no pressure angle. They stand lower than involute teeth, so the outside diameter is module × (teeth + 1.2). Round gears with the same module mesh, at the same centre distance as involute ones; with an involute gear they do not fit. “Simples” are the straight teeth every gear had so far. There you set “Tamanho do dente” and “Largura do dente” by hand. Older designs keep them until you change the tooth shape. All three tooth shapes have the “Furo central”. The “Coroa interna” has its teeth pointing in: a ring that a smaller gear runs inside, like the outer wheel of a planetary set. You set it like an involute or round gear by “Dentes”, “Módulo (mm)” and “Folga entre dentes”, plus the “Aro”, the ring outside the teeth. Its outside diameter is module × (teeth + 2.5) plus twice the rim, with round teeth module × (teeth + 1.7). A gear of the same module runs in it when its centre stands (ring teeth − its teeth) × module / 2 from the ring's centre; select both and the properties panel gives that distance. For a planetary set, ring teeth = sun teeth + 2 × planet teeth, for example 30 = 12 + 2 × 9. A ring gear has no centre hole, it is the ring itself. Between 26 and 33 teeth its tips are up to a quarter module shorter, because a tiny edge would otherwise form at the base circle; meshing is not affected. The “Cremalheira” is the gear of endless radius: a bar with teeth along one side, whose flanks are straight lines at the pressure angle with involute teeth. Its width (along X) is teeth × pitch, the pitch being π × module, so racks of one module line up end to end, each end falling in a gap. Its length (along Y) is the thickness of the bar and free, as long as the teeth and half a millimetre of bar fit in. The teeth point to the front, towards the viewer of the home view; turn the rack as you need it. A gear of the same module rolls on it when its centre stands its teeth × module / 2 in front of the pitch line; the pitch line lies a module behind the tooth tips, 0.6 module with round teeth. Ring gear and rack come with involute and with round teeth, not with simple ones; switching the gear type keeps the module. The edge tool and the STEP export take every gear as its exact body, involute flanks as smooth curves. A helical gear on an oval footprint stays a triangle mesh, and so does a helical gear with involute teeth from about 31 teeth. Small teeth limit how far edges can be rounded: on a gear with simple teeth, 30 mm across with 12 teeth the flat between two teeth at the foot is only about 0.65 mm wide, so rounding every edge works up to about 0.5 mm, and on a bevel gear, whose top is smaller, up to about 0.4 mm. A helical gear's teeth lean, which narrows that flat across its slanted edges: the larger the helix angle against the gear's height, the smaller the rounding that fits. The edges of its two flat ends can be rounded, but chamfering just those edges fails in the CAD kernel; round them, or chamfer all edges together at a smaller size, such as 0.2 mm.

The “Mola” has “Voltas” and a “Arame”. Together with the height they decide how soft the spring is. “Enrolamento” sets which way the wire runs: “Enrolamento à direita” like a usual compression spring, or “Enrolamento à esquerda”. The edge tool and the STEP export take a spring as its exact body: a round wire along a helix, cut square at both ends. You can round or chamfer those two wire ends, for instance.

A “Tubo curvado” consists of up to twelve sections: a straight piece followed by a bend. For each you set the “Comprimento reto”, the “Ângulo da curva”, the “Raio da curva” and the “Ângulo de giro”. The section you are editing is lit up in orange on the tube, so you can follow the order. A roll angle of 0° bends within the plane of the workplane, at 90° the tube bends upward. The profile can be round, square, hexagonal or octagonal, the inside likewise, or fully solid. If the tube runs into itself, PrintCaddy warns you.

The “Transição” joins one outline at the bottom to another at the top, like a loft in Fusion: a hose adapter from one diameter to another, a square fan onto a round duct, a stand that turns round towards the top. For each end you pick “Contorno inferior” and “Contorno superior”: “Círculo / elipse”, “Retângulo” with “Raio dos cantos inferiores”, or “Polígono” with its number of corners, plus the width and length of each end and the height. “Deslocamento do topo na largura” and “Deslocamento do topo no comprimento” move the top end sideways for a slanted transition; the bottom end stays where it is. “Espessura da parede (0 = maciço)” turns the solid body into a tube open at the top and the bottom. The opening is smaller by the wall at both ends, measured across; where the wall slants it is a little thinner. Drag the frame bigger and both ends grow along, while the corner radius and the wall keep their size. “Transição suave (%)” makes the transition smooth. At 0 the sides run straight from the bottom to the top, as on a cone. At 100 they leave both ends straight up and change their size in between along an S-curve: a hose adapter that flares smoothly from a narrow to a wide pipe, instead of running like a funnel. In between the slider mixes the two. A smooth transition works together with “Espessura da parede (0 = maciço)”, a twist, a tilt and a sideways offset; a tube with a wall stays open at both ends. It is an exact body like the straight one, so its edges can be chamfered and filleted, but it is built through several sections and takes a little longer to calculate. “Segmentos por círculo” sets how finely the circles and rounded corners are drawn: how many straight pieces a full circle is made of in the view and in STL, OBJ and 3MF. It starts at 96, which is smooth for most parts; for a large round end you want to see without facets, raise it, up to 360. More pieces mean larger files. A polygon keeps the “Cantos inferiores” you set. The field shows when an end is round or has a rounded corner. “Torção” turns the section evenly about the vertical on the way up, up to 360° either way; the sides then wind round. “Inclinação do topo, frente/trás” and “Inclinação do topo, esquerda/direita” tilt the top end, up to 45°: a positive value raises its front edge or its right side. The sections in between tilt by their share, so the wall runs smoothly into the slant. The highest point stays at the set height. If the height later becomes so small that the slanted end would reach under the plate, the tilt gives way until it fits. A bend along a path, such as a pipe elbow, is not something the loft does. The loft is an exact body, twisted and tilted too: its edges can be chamfered and filleted, and STEP export keeps it. Add a flange with screw holes as usual and group them.

The “Gridfinity” shape makes parts for the open storage system by Zack Freedman: bins on a 42 mm grid that stand in a baseplate and stack on one another. The measures follow the published Gridfinity specification, so a bin from PrintCaddy fits a baseplate made with another generator, and the other way round. Under “Tipo” you choose: “Caixa”: a bin with a foot under every grid unit. “Unidades na largura” and “Unidades na profundidade” count grid units of 42 mm (a bin is 0.5 mm smaller, 41.5 mm for one unit); “Unidades na altura” counts height units of 7 mm, up to 20. The “Borda de empilhamento” on top of the wall holds the feet of the next bin and makes the bin 4.4 mm taller: a bin of 3 units with the lip is 25.4 mm tall. With “Furos para ímãs” every foot gets a hole for a 6 × 2 mm magnet in each corner. “Base”: the plate the bins stand in, 5 mm tall, with a socket for every grid unit. It is an open frame with no floor and no magnet holes. “Bandeja”: a tray of any size with a flat bottom, for board game inserts and parts that need no grid. “Comprimento”, “Largura” and “Altura” are free in mm, 10 to 252 mm across and deep and 3 to 140 mm high. It has no feet, no stacking lip and no magnet holes, so it does not stand in a baseplate or stack, and its corners are rounded by 3.75 mm, as a bin's are. Everything below about a bin's inside works on a tray too: its floor is 1.2 mm thick until you set it, its dividers and label shelves run up to its top, they and its finger scoops come at any height that leaves them room, and it takes as many compartments as leave each at least 6 mm wide, up to 24 along a side and 40 in all. A bin turned into a tray keeps its size, a baseplate turned into one is 20 mm high, and a tray turned back into a bin or a baseplate is rounded to grid units; with “Bandeja” as the type under “Padrões das formas” in “Configurações da área de trabalho”, a new tray starts 80 mm wide, 40 mm long and 20 mm high. The size of a bin or baseplate is always whole grid units (or cells of 21 mm on the half-size grid below), up to 6 × 6 (252 mm, which fits a 256 mm print bed), plus a baseplate's padding (see below); a drag on a handle snaps to the nearest unit. The wall (0.95 mm), the floor (1.2 mm) and the depth of the magnet holes (2.4 mm) are not in the specification; the depth of the holes is fixed, and the wall and the floor can be set (see below). The sizes in this section are for the 0.95 mm wall. The specification's M3 screw holes are not made. The top of the lip is sharp, as the specification draws it; if your printer leaves it ragged, chamfer it with “Chanfro da borda de empilhamento”, up to 1 mm, which is the edge tool's chamfer of that size built in, or round it with the edge tool. A bin stacked on top rests on the lip's slope right up to the top, so a chamfer takes the top of that away: about a tenth at 0.25 mm and over a third at 1 mm. Bin, baseplate and tray are exact bodies, so fillet, chamfer and the STEP export work on them. To divide a bin, group thin boxes into it as walls: stand them on the floor, 5.95 mm up (1.2 mm in a tray, or on the raised floor), and on a bin with the lip keep their top at least 0.5 mm below 7 mm per height unit, measured from the underside of the bin (20.5 mm for 3 units), because the feet of the next bin reach 0.35 mm down into the bin. Print bins and baseplates without supports, standing as they are on the print bed. A bin can also be made on a half-size grid: switch on “Grade de meio tamanho (21 mm)”, and then “Unidades na largura” and “Unidades na profundidade” count cells of 21 mm, up to 12 (the same 251.5 mm as 6 units). Every cell has a foot of its own, 20.5 mm across at the top with the specification's steps, and four of them stand in one socket of an ordinary baseplate, so a bin of 1½ or 2½ units fits beside whole ones. When “Grade de meio tamanho (21 mm)” is switched on, the bin keeps its outline (2 units become 4 cells); when it is switched off, an odd number of cells is rounded up to whole units. The lip follows the bin's outline as before. With “Furos para ímãs” each foot gets one hole, 2.5 mm both ways from its middle towards the corner of its cell that lies on the 42 mm grid, counted from the bin's left back corner: the holes line up with those of a baseplate with magnets from another generator when that corner stands on a corner of the grid; a bin of an odd number of cells can also be turned by 180°, so that this corner stands on a corner of the grid at the front right. The baseplate stays on the 42 mm grid. The half-size grid is not part of the specification. A bin of 3 height units or more can have label shelves along its inner walls: switch on “Apoio de etiqueta atrás”, “Apoio de etiqueta na frente”, “Apoio de etiqueta à esquerda” or “Apoio de etiqueta à direita”, in any combination. Each shelf that is on gets its own “Largura do apoio”, “Comprimento do apoio” and, for a shorter shelf, “Posição do apoio”; the corner settings below them apply to all of them. A shelf is flat on top for a label, with a 1.2 mm strip down at the front and an underside rising at 36 degrees. Its top is 0.85 mm below 7 mm per height unit, measured from the underside of the bin (20.15 mm for 3 units), so the feet of a bin stacked on the lip stay 0.5 mm clear of it. A bin made lower than 3 units shows no shelves; they come back at 3 units. Label shelves are not part of the specification. “Largura do apoio” is how far a shelf reaches into the bin: 14 mm, at most 17.2 mm in a bin of 3 units (less with a raised floor), and 16.8 mm for two shelves facing each other in a bin 1 unit deep with 2 mm corners. With “Comprimento do apoio” at 0 a shelf runs from wall to wall. A shorter one, at least 10 mm, brings up “Posição do apoio”, which moves it from the middle of its wall: to the right on the back and front walls, as the front view shows them, and towards the front on the side walls. An end that comes within 1 mm of a wall (1.8 mm with the stacking lip, whose support leans in there), or that stops on that wall's shelf, runs on into it, and two shelves that meet in a corner join into one. Where a shelf meets a wall or another shelf and there is room, the corner is rounded or chamfered: choose “Redondos” or “Chanfrados” under “Cantos do apoio”, and the size with “Tamanho do canto” (2 mm; 0 leaves it sharp). With “Redondos”, a shorter shelf's free ends have their front corners rounded too, by the same size but at most half the shelf's width. A bin can also have a finger scoop along any of its inner walls, so that small parts can be pushed out up the curve instead of being picked out where the floor meets the wall: switch on “Curva para os dedos atrás”, “Curva para os dedos na frente”, “Curva para os dedos à esquerda” or “Curva para os dedos à direita”, in any combination. The floor rises along a quarter circle into the wall, from wall to wall, and two scoops on neighbouring walls meet in their corner. A bin with a scoop also has every floor edge rounded by 2.8 mm, the radius of its inner corners, and the scoop is that rounding made larger on its wall. Once a scoop is on, “Raio da curva” appears below the switches and applies to all of them: until you set it, it is half the height from the floor up to where the lip's support leaves the wall, 1.65 mm below 7 mm per height unit, measured from the underside of the bin, or up to the top of a bin without the lip (6.7 mm in a bin of 3 units with the lip, less with a raised floor). It is at least 3.5 mm and stays at least 0.5 mm less than that height, and across the bin it leaves at least 2 mm of floor, between two scoops facing each other or between a scoop and the wall opposite it. A bin of 1 height unit has no room for a scoop and shows no switches for it; they come back at 2 units. Finger scoops are not part of the specification either. A bin can also have a raised floor, for a bin blank to cut shapes into: “Altura do fundo” sets the floor's height, measured from the underside of the bin (5.95 mm, the 1.2 mm floor on the feet, until you set it), and the bin is solid up to it. With the lip it goes up to where the lip's support leaves the wall, 1.65 mm below 7 mm per height unit (19.35 mm for 3 units), so the lip stays whole and the feet of a bin stacked on it stay 1.3 mm clear; without the lip it goes up to the top, and the bin is a solid block. Group holes in the shapes of your tools into it, as deep as you need. Finger scoops start on the raised floor, and label shelves reach less far into the bin so that their underside still ends above the floor; once the floor leaves them no room, their switches go (the scoops above 15.35 mm, the shelves above 15.54 mm, in a bin of 3 units with the lip) and come back when you lower it. A bin of 1 height unit with the lip and a wall of 1.6 mm or less has no room to raise its floor and shows no field for it. A raised floor is not part of the specification either. “Espessura da parede” sets the wall in from the outside, which never changes, so the bin still fits and stacks as any other. It is 0.95 mm until you set it, from 0.8 mm (two lines of a 0.4 mm nozzle) up to where the walls meet. The inner corners are rounded by 3.75 mm less the wall, and square from a wall of 3.75 mm; the rounded floor edges follow them. With the lip, a wall over 1.75 mm stops at a flat ledge 0.85 mm below 7 mm per height unit, so a stacked bin's feet stay 0.5 mm clear, and the floor goes no higher than that ledge. Where the walls leave less than 1 mm inside, the bin is built solid and “Altura do fundo” is hidden. Finger scoops and label shelves without room are left out, and fewer compartments are built and offered. A bin open in full on all four sides has no wall to set. A bin switched open on all four sides is never built solid; a side whose wall leaves no room for its opening is open in full. On a bin, “Raio dos cantos” rounds its outer corners less than the specification's 3.75 mm, down to 0 for square ones, so bins side by side in a drawer leave only their 0.5 mm gaps where four of them meet. Only the outer wall takes it, from 0.5 mm over the feet up: the feet, the inside and the slopes of the lip a stacked bin rests on keep their rounding, so the bin fits in a baseplate and stacks as before, and a bin of one unit still sits down on the slopes of its socket. Over a square corner the wall ends flat, level with the top of the lip (the bin's top without one) or with the foot of its chamfer. A corner on an open side is square already. A bin can also be divided into compartments without grouping walls into it: under “Compartimentos”, just below “Propriedades”, “Colunas” and “Linhas” set how many, up to 4 per grid unit each way (2 per cell of the half-size grid) and 40 in all. The dividers run the full height, from the floor (or the raised floor) up to 0.85 mm below 7 mm per height unit, where the label shelves stop too, so a bin stacked on the lip sits as before. Dividers need a bin of 2 height units or more, with the floor at least 3 mm below their top; with less room the bin is built without them, and they come back once it has room again. “Espessura da divisória” is 1.2 mm until you set it, from 0.8 to 3 mm. The dividers start evenly spaced. To move one, pick it under “Entre colunas” or “Entre linhas”, counted from the left or from the back, and set its “Posição”, measured from the inside of the left or back wall to the middle of the divider; every compartment stays at least 6 mm wide. Once a divider has been moved, the dividers running that way keep their places in millimetres when the bin is resized; a new number of compartments spaces that way's dividers evenly again. Each compartment has the bin's inner corners, rounded by 2.8 mm, and its floor edges are rounded by 2.8 mm too, with or without a finger scoop. Finger scoops are repeated in every compartment: with a scoop on the back wall, each compartment has one on its back side, against the wall or a divider. In a narrow compartment the radius is made smaller so that 2 mm of floor stays flat, and a compartment too narrow even for 3.5 mm loses the scoops that run that way; a note under “Raio da curva” says so. Dividers are not part of the specification either. A bin with dividers can have a label shelf in each compartment instead of the shelves along its walls: those are for bins without compartments, and their switches come back once the bin is one compartment again. In a bin of 3 height units or more, choose a compartment with “Linha” and “Coluna” (each shown when there is more than one), and under “Apoio de etiqueta” the side its shelf stands against, the bin's wall or a divider; a side is only offered while a shelf there still leaves the compartment open. “Comprimento do apoio (%)” runs from 10 to 100; a shelf that would come out shorter than 4 mm is left out, and a note under it says so. A shorter shelf brings up “Posição do apoio”: “Esquerda”, “Meio” or “Direita” on a back or front side, or “Trás”, “Meio” or “Frente” on a left or right side. “Largura do apoio” is 14 mm until you set it, less in a narrow compartment, and a shelf never reaches so far that it closes its compartment off: at least 6 mm stays open in front of it. The shelves have the profile of those along the walls, and “Cantos do apoio” and “Tamanho do canto” under “Propriedades” apply to them as well. A bin can also be open on any side, so that bins standing side by side make one long run: switch on “Aberta atrás”, “Aberta na frente”, “Aberta à esquerda” or “Aberta à direita”, in any combination; with all four only the floor on its feet is left. An open side has no wall and no stacking lip above the floor. The walls beside it and their lip run straight out to the bin's outline and end square, so two open bins next to each other are 0.5 mm apart like any two bins, and the floor runs flat out to the edge and ends square there. A label shelf or finger scoop on an open side is not built and its switch goes, and so do that side's scoops against the dividers; the setting is kept for when you close the side again. Shelves and scoops on the walls beside it, and dividers that meet it, run out to the edge, and a compartment offers no label shelf on an open side; one already chosen there is left out, and a note under “Apoio de etiqueta” says so. The feet and the magnet holes stay as they are. A bin stacked on an open bin is held by the lip on the closed sides only. A bin without the lip whose floor is raised to the top is a solid block and shows no switches for open sides. Open sides are not part of the specification either. A side switched open can also be opened only partly, for a slot to reach into or a lower wall at the front. Under the switches, each open side has its own rows, named here for the front: “Profundidade na frente” is the opening's depth, measured down from the top of the lip (from the bin's top without the lip), at least 2 mm; “Largura na frente” its width along the side, at least 5 mm; “Posição na frente” its position, “Esquerda”, “Meio” or “Direita”; and, at an end, “Distância na frente” its distance from that end. To begin with the opening is the whole side down to the floor, which is the open side described above. A depth within 0.5 mm of the floor goes down to the floor, and a width within 0.5 mm of the whole side is the whole side. Anything less keeps the side's wall, its rounded corners and the lip, and cuts a notch with a flat bottom and square ends out of them: down to the floor a slot, across the whole side a lower wall. The opening stays on the straight part of the wall between the corners, or runs out to the edge beside a side that is open in full, where the wall has no rounded corner; a side whose straight part is shorter than 5 mm is open in full. The floor, the dividers and the lip on either side of the notch stay, so a bin stacked on it still sits on the lip, and the side's label shelf, finger scoop and compartment label shelves stay off as on any open side. On a bin built solid by its wall, a side switched open is open in full. A side opened partly still has a wall, so “Espessura da parede” stays even with all four sides switched open. Once a side is opened partly, “Cantos da abertura” (“Redondos” or “Chanfrados”) and “Tamanho dos cantos da abertura” (0, square, until you set it; up to 10 mm, the row offering as much as the largest corner takes) appear below the open sides' rows and round or chamfer the notches' corners seen from outside the wall, the two at the top and the two at the bottom, alike on every side opened partly. The top corners take the size first and the bottom ones what the depth leaves, so a size over half the depth leaves the bottom corners less, and they stay square once the top ones take all of it. Each corner takes as much of the size as the notch and the wall beside it leave room for, so on an opening placed at an end, the top corner there is no larger than the opening's distance from that end; where a corner would end just beside an edge of the wall, it is made up to 0.5 mm smaller to keep clear of it, and under 0.5 mm it stays square. An opening across the whole side has no top corners, and one run out to the edge beside a side open in full has none at that end. With the lip, a top corner is rounded or chamfered in full on the outer wall only, a little less under a chamfered lip; further in, where the lip slopes down, less. A baseplate can have padding, for a drawer that is not a whole number of grid units: “Faixa atrás”, “Faixa na frente”, “Faixa à esquerda” and “Faixa à direita” add a solid border at the plate's 5 mm height outside the grid, from 0 to 41 mm on each side. The grid stays whole units of 42 mm and moves away from the padded sides, and the outer corners keep their rounding unless “Raio dos cantos” changes it. The plate's size is the whole plate with its padding; a change of padding keeps the units, and dragging a side changes the units and keeps the padding. To fill a drawer, type its inside size into “Largura da gaveta” and “Profundidade da gaveta”: for each, the plate takes as many units as fit, up to 6, and splits what is left, less 0.5 mm so the plate drops in, evenly between the padding on the two sides of that direction; the two rows show the drawer the plate fills. A drawer 230 mm wide gives 5 units, 210 mm, and 19.5 mm of padding, 229.5 mm in all; check that the plate fits your print bed. A drawer that one plate on your bed cannot fill takes several baseplates side by side, each padded only on the sides that face the drawer's walls; set their padding with the padding rows. A bin keeps the padding settings and is built without them; they come back when it is made a baseplate again. Padding is not part of the specification either. Below the padding rows, “Raio dos cantos” sets the radius of the plate's four outer corners, 4 mm as the specification draws them, down to 0 for square corners that sit in a drawer's corners; a drawer whose inside corners are rounded takes a radius at least as large as theirs, up to 4 mm. The sockets keep their rounding, so bins fit as before.

The “Dobradiça” prints in one piece and moves afterwards (print-in-place): two leaves lying open flat on the plate, with alternating knuckles on one axis between them. The pin belongs to the back leaf and runs with play through the knuckles of the front one. You set the “Comprimento (eixo)”, the “Largura aberta” and the “Diâmetro do nó”, plus the number of “Nós” (odd, so the pin is held at both ends), the “Diâmetro do pino” and the “Espessura da aba”. “Folga” is the gap between the moving parts: around the pin, between the knuckles and in front of the leaves. With 0.4 mm a well-tuned printer usually breaks free with a small twist; if the parts fuse, raise it, if it wobbles too much, lower it. Print the hinge lying down as it appears on the plate, without supports. If you would rather use a pin of your own, such as a piece of filament or wire, which is smoother than a printed pin on a small hinge, choose “Sem pino (use o seu)” under “Tipo”: the printed pin is left out and the bore, the pin diameter plus the clearance, runs through every knuckle, the ends included. With “Ângulo de abertura” you fold the second leaf up about the pin to place the hinge as it stands in your design: 0° lies flat as it prints, 180° is closed. The knuckles stay where they are and the hinge remains one piece; remember to set it back to 0° before printing in place. You can add holes to the leaves or group them into a larger part, such as a lid. A hinge can also be made “Com cones” (under “Tipo”): every other knuckle then ends in cones that nest into conical recesses of the knuckles beside it. There is no pin and no long bridge that could sag, so it prints lying flat; the cones stand at 45°. It is a mesh, so chamfers and fillets do not work on it and the STEP export holds triangles, and it makes fewer knuckles where they would be too short for a cone. Instead of the number of knuckles you can give the “Largura do nó (máx.)”: the knuckles are then at most that wide and their number follows from the length; typing a number of knuckles takes the width away again. “Tipo” has three choices: “Com pino”, “Sem pino (use o seu)” (the bore for a pin of your own) and “Com cones”. With cones, “Diâmetro do cone” sets how big the cones are where they grow from their knuckle; bigger cones hold better, and by default they are as large as fits. The cone hinge has no pin and no bore, so its leaf may be as thick as the whole knuckle: set “Espessura da aba” to the knuckle diameter and the leaves lie flush with the knuckles; such a hinge opens about 90° and no further, because the thick leaves meet. For screwing the hinge on, set the “Screw holes per leaf”: up to six holes along the axis, at the “Hole diameter” you choose. Under “Holes” they are “Countersunk” by default, at 90° for countersunk screws, on the side that faces the other leaf when the hinge is closed, so the heads lie flush; “Straight” leaves them plain. Without further values the holes share the length evenly and sit in the middle of each leaf; “Hole spacing (along)” and “Hole spacing (across)” set them centre to centre, for instance to match a bought hinge you replace. Every hole keeps half a millimetre of leaf to the edges, the knuckles and the next hole; where fewer fit, there are fewer, and the field says so. “Corner radius” rounds the four outer corners of the leaves. With a pin or without, holes and corners stay exact in the STEP export and for the edge tool. Under “Leaf shape”, “Fingers” gives each knuckle its own finger, as wide as the knuckle, instead of a leaf on each side; the fingers of the two sides alternate like two combs. As no finger lies under a knuckle of the other side, the hinge folds all the way round, and with the style “Com cones” and fingers as thick as the knuckle (“Espessura da aba” up to the “Diâmetro do nó”) it closes flat, the fingers of one side between those of the other. No leaf joins the fingers of a side: with the printed pin they hang on it, with cones, or without the pin until your own goes in, they are loose pieces. Join each side to your model, for instance one comb to a box and the other to its lid, or group them with it. “Corner radius” then rounds the tips of the fingers; fingers take no screw holes.

“Flexi joints” turns a flat body into a figure that moves, such as a fish, a snake or a dragon, printed in one piece (print in place). You draw or build the body yourself, for instance from a sketch or an SVG you extrude. The tool cuts it across its length into links and puts a joint at every cut: one link carries an upright knuckle that is thicker in the middle than at its ends, the next one wraps round it with clearance. So the joint holds without fusing, and every slope is at 45°, so it prints without support. Between the links a wedge stays open, as wide as the links should swing to the side. Select the body (several parts are joined, holes among them cut away) and click “Flexi joints”. In the window you set along which side it is cut (“Longer side” takes the longer one), how many “Joints” there are, the “Clearance” (0.4 mm suits most printers) and the angle for “Swing to each side”. The joints are sized to the body; without “Joint size to fit the body” you give the “Joint diameter” yourself. Without “Links all the same length” you set how far the first joint lies from the start and the last from the end, so that a head, say, stays one large piece. Where a joint goes, the body should be about 6 mm high and 12 mm wide at least; if one does not fit, the window says which. The result is a bundle of links (meshes) that you print as it lies. If you do not like the cut, undo it and try other values. A first test print with two or three joints shows whether the clearance suits your printer.

The “Serrilhado” is a round grip with grooves all around, for knobs, thumb wheels and tool handles. Under “Padrão” you pick “Reto”, grooves along the axis as on a control knob, “Cruzado”: two slanted rows of grooves cross into small diamonds, or “Redondo”: grooves and ridges along the axis as a soft wave of arcs, a pleasant grip without sharp ridges. Round grooves stay shallower than half a pitch, or the ridges would bulge at their foot; a depth too great gives way. You set the “Diâmetro” and the “Altura”, the number of “Ranhuras” and the “Profundidade da ranhura”; for crossed knurling also the “Ângulo da ranhura” to the axis. The “Chanfro nas pontas” breaks both ends at 45 degrees, as on a turned knob; 0 leaves them sharp. Straight and round knurling are exact bodies, so their edges can be broken and rounded. Crossed knurling stays a mesh, because as an exact body it would take almost a minute to compute with 30 grooves. For a knob on a shaft, group the knurl with a hole, such as a “Rosca” set as a tapped hole. Grooves shallower than 0.4 mm hardly any printer prints cleanly, and PrintCaddy does not set them closer than 0.8 mm around the grip: a thin grip gets fewer of them.

The “Rabo de andorinha” is the joint in which two parts lock into each other and can only be slid together sideways. You set the width at the wide end, the “Largura do pescoço” and the length of the tail. Copy the tail for the other side and make the copy a hole: “Folga como orifício” then gives a little play so the joint does not jam after printing. Tip: A tapped hole cuts into the part it overlaps when grouped. So put it a bit into the material rather than just touching the surface.

A hole lying on its side gets a bridge across its top when printed, and the bridge sags. The “Furo em gota” therefore has a point on top: every layer rests on the one below, and the hole comes out round enough without supports. Set the “Diâmetro (parte redonda)” to the size of the hole, about 3.4 mm for an M3 screw, and the “Comprimento do furo” long enough to reach through the part. The “Ângulo da ponta” is 90°, so the flanks meet at 45°. Most printers handle that cleanly; a flatter point needs more height, a steeper one saves it. Make the teardrop a hole and group it with the part. Its length runs along the depth and the point faces up. For a hole in the other direction, turn it by 90° around the vertical axis. A tapped hole on its side sags at the top in the same way. Give it a teardrop of its own: add a “Furo em gota” hole whose “Diâmetro (parte redonda)” is the core of the thread, the diameter its teeth leave free (about 8.4 mm for M10), the same length as the tapped hole, and select both. Click “Alinhar” and bring them into line in the middle - the middle of the teardrop is the middle of its round part, not of its box with the tip, so the two circles lie on each other - and group both with the part. The thread is cut as usual and the tip opens the top of the hole, so it prints without supports.

A screw head often should not stand proud. The “Rebaixo” cuts a round pocket for a socket-head screw (DIN 912), the “Escareado” a cone for a countersunk screw (DIN 7991). Both stand with the head end up: the “Diâmetro da cabeça” is the diameter of the pocket or the cone, the “Diâmetro do corpo” the bore below it, the “Comprimento total” the whole length. On the counterbore you set the “Profundidade da cabeça”, on the countersink the “Ângulo do cone” (90° suits countersunk screws). The defaults fit an M3 screw. The “Escareado duplo” is a hole chamfered on both faces, for a plate that is to look neat on its front and its back. It has no entry of its own in the shape library: take the “Escareado” and switch on “Dos dois lados” in its properties (bodies that are a double countersink already show the switch on): a cone at each end opens to the “Diâmetro da cabeça”, with the “Diâmetro do corpo” between them. You set the “Ângulo do cone” and the “Comprimento total” as before. If the hole is too short for two full cones, they meet in the middle at that angle and the shaft stays wider than you set: a head of 10 mm, a shaft of 6 mm, 90° and a length of 2 mm make two cones from 10 down to 8 mm. As a hole it is pushed through a part like the others. Make the shape a hole and group it with the part. Let its top end a little above the surface the head should sit on, so the pocket opens cleanly. For the pocket of a hex nut, use a “Polígono” with six sides as a hole.

Tape measure, ruler and framing square, distances to the origin, notes that stay attached to a part, and reference points that things snap to. To build a part exactly, you need to measure. PrintCaddy has several tools for that. None of them ends up in an export. Wall thickness and gaps inside a part are best measured in the section view with “Medir”.

The tape measure sits at the lower end of the camera bar on the left edge (“Trena”). It measures distances between corners, edges and faces. A click on it opens five buttons. If they cover what you want to measure, drag them by the grip on the left anywhere on the workplane; a double-click on the grip puts them back: The tape measure with its buttons: add measurement, move measuring points, remove measurement, whole edges, delete all measurements. “Adicionar medida”: Click one point, drag to the next and click it. The distance is labelled, with the axes it runs along in front: X, Y or Z for a straight one, XY, XZ or YZ across a plane, 3D for all three. Hover over the label to see how far it reaches along each axis, over a point to see its coordinates. While you place the second point, the axes, the distance and the reach along each axis show beside the pointer. A measurement that lies mostly behind another body fades; hovering its line or label brings it back. On an opposing edge or face, the second point snaps in at a right angle to the first when the pointer comes near - or anywhere on that edge or face while you hold Shift. Along the same face or on the workplane, Shift keeps the measurement straight along the main axis. “Mover pontos da medida”: Grab the points and move them, the number follows. “Excluir parte da medida”: Afterwards click a measurement to remove it. While “Adicionar medida” is active, holding Shift or Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and clicking a measurement point or line deletes it right away without switching modes. “Medir arestas inteiras”: A click on an edge measures all of it, the length of a circle for example. With this switched off, a click puts a point on the edge instead, and the second point goes anywhere, so you can measure the diameter or any other distance. Alt turns the switch round for one click. On a circle, the point across from the first one snaps in when the pointer comes near, and the points sit on the true circle, so the diameter comes out exact. “Excluir todas as medidas”: Removes every measurement at once. Because this cannot be undone, PrintCaddy asks first; with no measurements there is nothing to do. “Marcar o meio como ponto de referência”: In the middle of every measurement sits a small round mark, its lower half filled. It puts a reference point in the middle of the measurement: after a click on a round edge, such as the rim of a hole, in the centre of that circle - on an imported mesh too, where nothing else marks the middle of a hole - and for a diameter or any straight measurement halfway along it. A shape you drag then snaps to the point with its centre. A point that is there already is not made twice. The tape measure snaps to a reference point like to a corner, so you can measure from the centre of a circle or from the middle of a line: mark it, then click the point. “Digite um comprimento: o corpo no segundo ponto se move ao longo da linha; um comprimento negativo o leva além do primeiro ponto”: When at least one end of a straight measurement sits on a body, its number can be clicked. Type a new length and press Enter: the body at the second point moves along the measured line until the distance is exactly that, as with the ruler in Tinkercad. If only the body at the first point is selected, that one moves instead. The measuring points stay on the body, so the measurement follows. Measure from a corner, an edge or a reference point, such as the centre of a circle, to place parts at an exact distance. A negative length takes it that far past the first point, say 5 mm inside the edge of a box. Esc leaves measuring mode.

You fetch the “Régua” from the shape library. It is purely a measuring tool: it appears in no export and can neither be grouped nor cut. For every body that touches or overlaps the ruler, it shows the extent as a floating number right in the view. You can change that number right there, and the body follows. Stand the ruler up or tip it, and it measures along its own direction: upright beside a body it shows the body's height. The floating plus symbol creates a copy of the measured shape; it is there while the ruler lies flat. Its printed scale is in millimetres along one long edge, with the tens numbered, and in inches along the other, with a line every sixteenth of an inch and the whole inches numbered. The scale of the unit you work in (the switch at the bottom right) runs along the top edge; a ruler narrower than 15 mm carries only that one.

Sometimes you measure better at a right angle. Click “Posicionar esquadro” in the camera bar and then the workplane. A framing square with two arms at a right angle, with tick marks like a try square, is placed there. It has no body of its own either. Click close to the corner of a body, and its corner snaps exactly there. The design keeps the square where you set it, also in a saved .lyl file: when you open the design again, it is in the same place, turned the same way and measuring from the same points, until you remove it. The framing square lies on the workplane. If that sits on the side of a body, the square lies on that side too, see View and workplane. That is how you dimension on a vertical wall: put the workplane on the wall, place the square at its top left corner and click the handle until the arms point right and down. Dragging the handle moves it. A short click on the handle turns it by 90°. The × beside it removes it. The small button left of the handle switches what is measured from: the outside of a body (endpoint, an icon with lines) or its middle (midpoint, a crosshair). A small switch of the same kind sits beside each green number and sets that number alone: for a standing cylinder the middle in the two arms and the bottom in height, for a lying one the middle across and an end along. When all three agree again, the button at the handle shows the common mode. If bodies stand at one of the arms, the framing square shows their dimensions automatically, selected or not: bodies inside the square, beside an arm or across it. A body outside it, behind the corner or beside an arm from the outside, gets none. That works on the base plate only, not on the side of a body. The button with the arrow under the square's handle switches that off, so that only the selected bodies show their dimensions; it is kept with the design. When you select a body, the framing square shows in green how far it is from the corner, along both arms and in height. Click a green number to type a distance, and the body moves exactly there. With several bodies selected, they count as one: the ruler measures their shared outline, and a typed value moves them all together without changing their positions relative to each other. The guide lines of the green numbers run along the floor, the plane the framing square lies in, to the point below or beside the body; the height has its own arrow. The switch of each number sits in the frame of the number. The arms and the ticks are lines in the room: a body in front of them hides them, as a real square would be hidden. The small eye below the handle switches that: with the eye struck through, bodies hide the square (the start); with the eye open, the square stays in view over everything. The numbers on the arms fade where a body stands in front of them. With the midpoint, the green numbers count to the middle of the body, in height as well. That way you place a sphere with its centre exactly 15 mm from an edge, without subtracting the radius. On a wall you place a hole 40 mm from the left and 190 mm from the top like this: select the hole, switch to midpoint, type 40 and 190. The height there counts outward from the wall. Both the tape measure and the framing square stay where they are while you sketch and come back to the 3D view. Neither is in the history. The framing square is kept with the design, and so are the measurements of the tape measure, in the browser and in the .lyl file: they are there again when you open the design. The eye button among the tape measure's buttons hides all measurements and shows them again; whether they are hidden is kept as well, and adding, moving or deleting a measurement shows them first.

h: Distances to the origin and while moving
t: In the settings under “Aparência” there are two switches for live dimensions: “Mostrar dimensões do deslocamento” shows by how much you move while dragging. That includes lifting with the black arrow above a body; the way up or down shows at its front corner. Once you let go, click such a number and type the exact distance; a minus goes down. “Mostrar distâncias até a origem” shows the distances of the selection to the origin of the plate, also with several selected bodies. With “Dimensões sempre visíveis” the dimensions stay visible permanently. For a moment without them, press Q: the sizes and distances around the selection disappear, so a part you move is easy to see. Q again brings them back. A handle you point at still shows its size.

A note records what the geometry does not say: "This screw is 0.3 mm too tight", "print the lid yet", "dimension from Peter". Place one with “Anotação” or the N key. If you place the note on a body, it travels with it. If you place it beside, it stays on the workplane (“No plano de trabalho”). “Soltar do objeto” releases an attached note from the body. “Grupo de união” takes an attached note into the group; “Desagrupar” hands it to the visible part under it, a group inside included. While a group is open with “Editar grupo”, its notes move with the part under them and go back to the group with “Concluído”; cancelling puts them back as they were. If its body is deleted, or no visible body is under it any more, the note stays where it stood, on the workplane. Dragging the pin moves the note. A click on the pin folds the card away, only the small number stays; another click opens it again. A click into the text edits it. While you write, Enter keeps the text and Esc puts it back to how it was before you started; Shift+Enter starts a new line. In a sketch, “Anotação” (under “Gerenciar”) or N places a note too, anywhere on the sketch. All of a sketch's notes belong to its body: in the 3D view they sit on it, on the top of an extruded or swept body and on the drawn profile of a revolved one, and move with it. When you open the sketch again it shows the body's notes, including those placed in 3D. In the sketch, Undo takes back a note like a line, and “Cancelar” discards what you changed in the notes. Shift+N shows or hides the notes here too. Notes are saved in the design, appear in no export and can be shown or hidden with “Mostrar anotações e pontos” (in “Opções de visibilidade”, the arrow beside the eye icon) or with Shift+N.

A reference point is a bare mark in space, like a pencil mark or a layout point in a workshop: it belongs to no body, is never printed, and other things snap to it. Right-click a body and choose “Marcar o centro”, “Marcar os cantos” or “Marcar os meios das arestas”: the points appear on the top face of the body (of the whole selection, if you selected several). “Marcar o centro desta face” puts one in the middle of the flat face you right-clicked instead, on a side or an end, say. With a pivot set, “Marcar o pivô” puts one exactly on it, so another part's centre snaps to the point the selection turns about. Drag a point to move it: it snaps to the corners, the middles of the edges and faces of bodies, to their real corners and to other points; hold Alt to let it go free. Or click it to see its coordinates and type new ones; they use the unit you set. Each card can be dragged away by its title if it covers something, on its own: the others stay where they are, and a double-click on the title puts it back. The card you touched last stands in front of the others. Delete all in a card, or Delete all reference points in the right-click menu (of a body, or of an empty spot of the 3D view), deletes every point at once. “Excluir” removes it. The tape measure can mark a point too: “Marcar o meio como ponto de referência”, the half-filled mark in the middle of a measurement, puts one in its middle, in the centre of a round hole for example. And it measures from a point: the tape snaps to reference points like to corners. When you drag a shape, its edges and its centre snap to a point, like they snap to other shapes (“Encaixar em outras formas ao mover”). The framing square snaps to points too. Points are saved in the design, appear in no export, and are shown or hidden together with the notes by “Mostrar anotações e pontos” (Shift+N). An AI can mark, list and remove them with layerling_add_reference_points, layerling_list_reference_points and layerling_remove_reference_points.

A reference image is a picture to line parts up on: lay a photo of a circuit board on the floor of its case, and place the standoffs, holes and connector cut-outs right on it. It is a guide, not a body: it is never printed, never exported (STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP, SVG), never part of a group, a bundle or a cut, and the print estimate leaves it out. Open “Importar” and choose “Imagem de referência”, then a PNG, JPG, WebP, GIF or BMP picture. It lands on the workplane - on the plate, or on the face you set the workplane on - with its longer side 100 mm, half see-through. Move, turn and resize it with its handles like any shape. A body in front of it is picked first, so working on top of it does not grab the picture. “Transparência (%)” in its settings fades it from solid to barely there. “Calibrar” gives it its true size, as in the sketch: click two points on the picture whose real distance you know - two mounting holes of the board, say - and type that distance in “Distância real (mm)”. The picture keeps its proportions and its middle. Lock it with the lock in the header of its settings, and it stays put: clicks then go through it to the plate. Pick it in the object list to unlock it. The picture is saved once in the design file, however often it is copied or undone.
