A large picture makes the file larger by as much; the message when you add it says how large it is. An AI adds, moves, calibrates, fades and locks one with layerling_reference_image.
Como escolher a sua impressora, ser avisado quando algo não cabe e deitar a peça do jeito certo.

Abra as configurações (a engrenagem na área “Gerenciar” da barra de opções, “Configurações da área de trabalho”) e vá para a área “Plano de trabalho”. Em “Impressora” você escolhe a sua impressora numa lista de mais de 220 modelos comuns, entre eles Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Anycubic, Elegoo e muitos outros. As configurações do plano de trabalho com uma impressora escolhida. A mesa de impressão e a altura máxima de impressão vêm do perfil do fatiador. Três coisas acontecem: O plano de trabalho assume o tamanho da mesa de impressão. No canto do plano de trabalho aparecem o nome da impressora e o volume de impressão dela. Se o texto atrapalhar, desligue-o com “Textos na mesa” em “Plano de trabalho”; isso vale também para o nome do projeto, na frente à esquerda. PrintCaddy avisa quando algo não cabe. Os perfis de impressora vêm do OrcaSlicer, então são os mesmos que o seu fatiador conhece. Se preferir trabalhar sem impressora, escolha “Sem impressora - tamanho livre”. Você também pode definir o tamanho do plano de trabalho à mão.

Um sólido que passa da borda da mesa de impressão fica marcado. Uma mensagem diz quais lados passam e quanto. O mesmo vale se a peça for alta demais: a altura conta a partir do sólido mais baixo, do mesmo jeito que o fatiador apoia o modelo na mesa. A caixa é mais larga que a mesa de impressão da Bambu Lab A1 mini. A mensagem embaixo diz quanto ela passa. O aviso não impede você de continuar trabalhando. É uma dica, para você não descobrir só no fatiador que a peça é grande demais. Uma peça grande demais muitas vezes pode ser dividida: corte-a em duas com “Dividir” e imprima as duas metades separadamente. Se você deixa peças ao lado da mesa de propósito, clique no pequeno X da mensagem. O aviso então some só para esses sólidos. Se um deles voltar a caber e depois você o tirar da mesa de novo, ou se outro sólido passar da borda, a mensagem volta. Sólidos ocultos nunca contam, então ocultar as peças deixadas ao lado também funciona.

h: Deitando a peça do jeito certo
t: O jeito como a peça fica na mesa decide a resistência e a aparência dela. Duas ferramentas na área “Organizar” ajudam: “Deitar sobre a face”: clique numa face e a peça fica com esse lado para baixo. A melhor direção de impressão em um clique. “Baixar até o plano de trabalho” (D): apoia a peça no plano de trabalho quando ela está flutuando em algum lugar no ar. Algumas regras práticas para a direção de impressão: Faces grandes e planas para baixo. Elas aderem melhor. Deite peças compridas que sofrem esforço de modo que as camadas não fiquem perpendiculares à carga. É entre as camadas que a peça é mais fraca. Evite saliências mais inclinadas que 45°, ou adicione suportes a elas no fatiador.

No menu ao lado do olho (“Visibilidade”), Mostrar saliências liga a exibição das saliências. Toda face que aponta para baixo com inclinação maior que 45° fica então hachurada em vermelho e branco: é ali que a impressora precisaria de suportes. O que está apoiado na mesa fica sem marcação. Assim você vê, enquanto modela, se uma esfera, um arco ou um furo horizontal imprime sem suportes; o furo em gota foi feito exatamente para isso. Gire a peça ou deite-a sobre outra face com “Deitar sobre a face”, e a hachura acompanha na hora. A inclinação que a sua impressora aguenta é definida nas configurações, em “Aparência”: de 30° (cuidadoso) a 70° (para impressoras com boa refrigeração da peça). Uma face apoiada em outro sólido continua marcada: PrintCaddy só olha para a própria face.

h: Espessura de parede, folga e chanfros
t: As paredes devem ter pelo menos a largura de duas linhas de extrusão, ou seja, 0,8 mm com um bico de 0,4 mm. Peças resistentes precisam de 1,2 a 2 mm. Onde duas peças se encaixam uma na outra, é preciso folga: normalmente de 0,2 a 0,4 mm, dependendo da impressora. Faça um pequeno par de teste antes de imprimir a peça grande. Muita gente faz um chanfro leve na aresta de baixo, a que fica sobre a mesa. Isso evita que a primeira camada se espalhe ("pé de elefante").

Escolha “Exportar” e depois STL ou 3MF. STL é o formato mais simples. 3MF guarda os nomes e as cores de cada sólido e por isso é prático quando você imprime em várias cores. A janela de exportação também mostra quantos gramas e metros de filamento a peça gastaria impressa maciça. Mais em Arquivos e salvamento.
Where your designs live, how to back them up, which formats PrintCaddy imports and exports, and what is possible on a shared server.

PrintCaddy saves everything in the browser on your computer. There is no account and nothing is uploaded. (With a copy you host yourself, designs can live in a shared folder on the server instead; see the section on the shared folder further down.) Every change saves itself. The preview picture on the start page shows the view you last had in front of you when you went back with “Página inicial”. If you open PrintCaddy in the same browser days later, everything is there. If you go back to the start page from a design with nothing in it, PrintCaddy asks whether to keep it. “Sim” or Enter keeps it, “Não” removes it, so empty designs do not pile up. For a design in a shared folder on a server, “Não” deletes the file from the server, for everyone who uses it. That has a downside: whoever clears the browser storage or switches to another computer loses the designs. So back up important work into a file.

With dozens of designs a single list is not enough. On the start page, “Nova pasta” makes a folder for the designs of this browser; a click on the folder opens it. Folders can hold folders. Into a folder: drag a design onto the folder, or choose “Mover para …” in the design's menu, which lists every folder. A new design, and a file you open or import, made while a folder is open lands in that folder. Out again: the first tile in a folder, .., and the line under the tabs lead back; you can drop a design on them too. A folder dragged onto another folder goes inside it. Rename and delete are in the folder's menu. Deleting a folder deletes no design: what was in it moves one level up. Search looks through every folder; a design that is found shows its folder, and a click on it opens the folder. “Fazer backup de tudo” keeps the folders: the designs sit in the backup file in their folders, and restoring the backup puts them back there. The folders of this browser are separate from the folders on a server. The card pictures go into the file too, so they are back as soon as you restore.

On the start page every design has a menu with the options to rename, duplicate and delete. The row beside the tabs has the same buttons on every tab. To delete several designs at once, click “Selecionar”: a click on a card chooses it (a tick shows what is chosen), “Selecionar todos” chooses every design in the list, and “Excluir” asks once for all of them. “Concluído” or Esc leaves the selection. With “Fazer backup de tudo” you pack all designs of the open tab into one single ZIP file. “Restaurar backup”, beside it (it is there on a new computer with no designs, too), brings them back, also in another browser or on another computer; “Abrir um projeto ou importar geometria” takes the same file. The “Formas personalizadas” travel in the same file, in the folder Custom shapes, see Shapes. If you restore a backup into a browser that already has some of these designs, those are not added a second time; the notice says how many were already there. A design that cannot be read is left out, and the notice names it. If the page reloads in the middle of a backup, usually because a very large design took all the memory the browser allows, the start page says afterwards at which design it stopped: save that one on its own as a file (see below) or simplify its largest meshes, then back up again. Above the designs of this browser, a short line reminds you that they are kept nowhere else. Only some designs: after “Selecionar”, “Fazer backup” packs just the chosen designs, in their folders, into one ZIP file, and “Fazer backup” in a folder's menu packs that folder with every design and folder in it. Neither takes the custom shapes along, and “Restaurar backup” brings both back like a full backup. This is for the designs of this browser. You back up a single design in the editor: “Exportar”, choose the format LYL and click “Salvar projeto do PrintCaddy”. The LYL file is PrintCaddy's own design format and contains everything: shapes, groups, sketches, CAD data, imported sources and the history, meaning the undo steps. Under “Histórico de ações salvo” you choose how many of the last steps travel along; it starts at what the settings (the cogwheel in the ribbon) keep under “Histórico”. The last stop, “Nenhum”, saves the design with its current state only - the way to share a file without its undo steps. The export is a copy under the “Nome do arquivo” you give it; the design in your browser keeps its history. Older .skf files from earlier versions can still be opened; they are then saved as .lyl. Saving into your own folder (Chrome and Edge). There the button opens your system's save dialog, so you pick the folder and the name yourself, and an existing file can be replaced. Afterwards Ctrl+S saves the design into that same file again, without a dialog. A design opened from a .lyl file with “Abrir um projeto ou importar geometria” or the open button of the export window saves back into that file, too. The browser may ask once for permission to change the file. After the page is reloaded the design forgets its file, and the next Ctrl+S asks for it again; the dialog starts in the folder you used last. Firefox and Safari do not allow a page to write into files like this. There the file is downloaded to the Downloads folder as before, and Ctrl+S downloads it again; Firefox can be set to ask for the folder each time under Settings, General, Downloads.

Instructions, a parts list, notes, a photo or a datasheet can stay with the design as files. “Anexos” in the “Gerenciar” toolbar, the paperclip, opens the list; a small dot on the paperclip shows that the design has some. “Enviar anexo”: Choose one or more files: .md (Markdown) or .txt as plain text (UTF-8), .png, .jpg, .jpeg or .webp pictures, or .pdf documents. A file is checked by its content, so a file that is not what its name says is refused, and other types, .svg among them, cannot be attached. A text file can be at most 2 MB, a picture 16 MB and a PDF 32 MB; a design holds up to 32 files and 64 MB together. The list: The arrow downloads a file as it was uploaded. The bin removes it; the row asks once more first, and a removed file cannot be brought back with undo, because attachments are not part of the undo history. Reading a file: The eye on the row of a .md or .txt file opens it in a window to read, without downloading it. Markdown is shown formatted, with headings, lists, tick boxes, tables and code; a text file is shown exactly as it is written. Only links to web pages and e-mail addresses work, and they open in a new tab. Pictures named in the file are not loaded: their description stands in their place. Escape, the cross or a click beside the window closes it. Reading works in the History view too. Looking at a picture: The eye on the row of a picture opens it in the same window, shrunk to fit when it is large. A PDF has no eye: download it and open it in the program you read PDF files with. A name that is already there: PrintCaddy asks what to do. “Substituir” puts the new content into the file of that name, which keeps its place in the list. “Renomear” adds the new file under another name and suggests the first free one, such as notes 2.md. The cross leaves the new file out. Upper and lower case count the same, and the same file uploaded again changes nothing. Attachments are saved with the design like everything else: in the browser, in a LYL file, in a backup and in a design on a server, which they reach as soon as one is added or removed. They do not come along with “Inserir neste projeto” or with a custom shape, and a bug report does not contain them. A design with attachments is saved as a newer kind of LYL file: an older PrintCaddy says that it cannot open it instead of dropping the files. A design without attachments is saved exactly as before.

Click “Exportar” or press Ctrl+E. If the window covers something, drag it by its title bar to another spot; the Import and Attachments windows move the same way. A double click on the title bar puts it back. The export window with the formats STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP, SVG, PNG, LYL and 2D. At the top is the file name, below it you choose the format. With something selected, only the selection is exported, otherwise the whole design. If the selection leaves out visible parts, a note in the window says so plainly, and “Selecionar tudo” selects everything visible in one click. Once the file is written, the window closes by itself; if the export fails, it stays open with the message. Format For What to know STL slicer and 3D printing A triangle mesh. The simplest and most widespread format. An STL has no parts: bodies that overlap are joined into one mesh. To keep them as separate parts, export 3MF. In Chrome and Edge the first STL export asks where to save, and later STL exports of the design write into that file, until you type another name in the file name field or press “Salvar como…”. 3MF slicer with colours Every body stays a part of its own with name and colour. Overlapping bodies are only joined when they share a colour; where a shape sits inside one of another colour, say a logo in a plate, the one built first leaves room for the later one. Suited to PrusaSlicer, Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer and Cura. Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer ask on opening how to map the colours onto your filaments, and call the file "not from Bambu" - the message is harmless. OBJ modelling and exchange A widely supported mesh format. Colours are stored as vertex colours in the same file, with no extra .mtl. Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer read them and ask, as with 3MF, how to map them onto your filaments; other programs see only the shape. As with 3MF, overlapping bodies are only joined when they share a colour. STEP a full CAD program Keeps boxes, cylinders, spheres and cones as exact geometry, and so shapes made from an outline (star, heart, ellipse, tube, half sphere, round roof, rounded box, dovetail, the bores and more), the bent tube, threads, springs and gears, plus fillets and chamfers. The first STEP export in a session loads the CAD kernel (about 22 MB) once. SVG laser cutter and plotter A clean top view in millimetres, including holes and curved outlines. Under “Vista”, “Pegada no plano de trabalho” writes only the outlines where the objects stand on the workplane. “Arestas visíveis de cima” writes the edges you see from above as lines, each body in its colour; see below. DXF laser cutting shop The same top view (“Silhueta vista de cima” or “Pegada no plano de trabalho”) as one outline of lines, true arcs and circles - no polylines, splines or curves made of short straight pieces - on layer 0 in white, DXF 2000 in millimetres, not mirrored. Bodies that touch become one outline, so no line is cut twice. Shops ask for one part per file: select the part before exporting. Not yet tried on a laser cutter: feedback is welcome. PNG forum posts, print sites, questions A picture of the view as it is, at twice the resolution and without handles, selection frames and dimensions. “Mostrar a mesa de impressão” and “Fundo transparente” are chosen in the window. Turn and zoom first until the picture is right; the selection does not matter here. LYL PrintCaddy itself The editable design with everything that belongs to it. 2D workshop, lathe and mill, documentation A drawing at 1:1 as PDF or SVG: front, top and right-side views on an ISO sheet. See below. Bridges for parts that would fall out (DXF and SVG). When a plate with text is cut by a laser or a plotter, the middle of letters like o, a and b falls out. Tick “Pontes para manter as partes internas presas” in the export window of the DXF, or of the SVG with the top view, and small bridges hold such parts to the material round them, as on a stencil: “Largura da ponte” (0.5 to 3 mm) and “Pontes por parte” (1 to 4) are set beside it. A bridge never touches another outline or another bridge and never leaves a gap too narrow to cut; parts that would only hold each other are tied to the plate too. If a part gets no bridge at the chosen width, the message after the export says how many. Nothing changes unless the box is ticked. STL into your own folder (Chrome and Edge). There the first STL export of a design opens your system's save dialog, so you pick the folder and the name yourself and can replace an existing file. After that every STL export of the design writes into that same file without a dialog; the export window shows which file, and Save as… next to the export button picks another. The dialog remembers its own folder, apart from the one for designs, so the slicer files can stay with the slicer. After the page is reloaded the design forgets its STL file and the next export asks again. Firefox and Safari download the file as before. If you would rather have every STL as a plain download, so that the browser numbers a name it has already used (name (1).stl, name (2).stl) as Tinkercad does, switch on “Salvar STL como um download” in the settings under “Aparência”. A hole you have not grouped is taken out of every body it reaches when you export, as the view shows it. So there is no need to group before each export. With a selection, only the selected holes count. A hole cannot be exported on its own; PrintCaddy points that out. STEP only carries exact CAD bodies. What cannot be written exactly, such as a mesh imported as STL, is left out. The message after the export names those bodies and says why. For the printer, use STL or 3MF, which carry everything.

h: SVG for a laser or plotter
t: With “Arestas visíveis de cima” under “Vista”, the SVG shows the design as you see it from above, like the top view of a drawing: every edge you can see is a line, and edges hidden by other parts are left out. Each line has the colour of its body, so a laser or plotter program that sorts by colour puts each colour on a layer of its own. Whether a layer is cut, scored or engraved, you choose there. Every area a colour shows has a closed outline, and where two bodies meet, both get the line. The areas are filled even-odd, so filling a colour to engrave it leaves its holes and the places of other bodies free. A part reaching through another gets the line where it comes out. The SVG is at 1:1 in millimetres, with the front of the design at the bottom of the page, in the same place as the silhouette. A design with too many edges for this view, such as a plate with hundreds of holes, gets its filled silhouette instead, and the message after the export says so.

Choose the format 2D (hover over it and it says Drawing) and, below the file name, PDF or SVG. With something selected, only the selection is drawn, otherwise the whole visible design; holes you have not grouped still cut the parts they reach. PrintCaddy draws the front, top and right-side views in first-angle layout (the right side to the left of the front view, the top view below it) on the smallest ISO sheet that fits, from A4 to A0, or a larger one if the part needs it. It is always at 1:1. Each view carries its overall width and height, and edges you cannot see are dashed. Round bores that run parallel to a view direction get a centre cross and a label (F1, T1, R1), and a table at the bottom lists their diameter and position, measured from the lower-left corner of the view. The title block in the lower-right corner holds the name, scale, units, date and sheet number. The words on the sheet follow the interface language. Print at 100 % or "actual size", or the lengths will not match. What the drawing does not do: threads, depths, tolerances and bores at an angle are not dimensioned, and the sizes come from the model as a mesh, so they are nominal. A very detailed part (over 100,000 triangles) or more than 200 bores is refused with a message; choose fewer objects then. The projection is based on the drawing work of Cadverix-3D by WC3D.

h: How much filament does it take?
t: For STL, 3MF, OBJ and STEP the “Material” box shows the volume, weight and length of 1.75 mm filament of what is exported. It counts like the file: visible bodies only, holes taken off, overlaps only once. On the right you pick the filament - PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, TPU or PA (nylon) - and the weight follows its density. The volume is the body's own. Weight and filament are a rough estimate for a print with walls and infill: you set the “Preenchimento” (15 % to begin with) and the “Paredes” (2) under the heading, and the box says what it counted and what the same part would weigh solid. Your slicer's own settings decide the real number, so take it as a guide: good for comparing designs and for whether the spool will last. At 100 % infill the box counts the part as solid, the upper bound. The box works out its numbers when you press “Calcular”, so the export window opens at once even for a finely traced model.

With “Importar” or Ctrl+I you bring foreign files into the design. The import window: open or insert designs and drop geometry. “Abrir projeto do PrintCaddy”: A PrintCaddy design (.lyl, or an older .skf) comes back as a new design. “Inserir neste projeto”: The bodies of a PrintCaddy design are added to the open one. Handy for basic shapes you need again and again: build them once, save them and bring them in every time. Drop one or more .lyl files on the drop zone below and they are inserted the same way. Its notes come along, closed and numbered on after the ones already in the design, and so do its reference points. DXF: A DXF, as a laser cutting shop or a supplier sends a part outline, comes in as parts to work on: every closed outline a body 4 mm high and every hole in it a hole of its own beside it (a round one a cylinder), so a hole is moved and sized in the 3D editor like any other; select them all to move the part. In millimetres (a file in inches is converted, one without a unit is read as millimetres), arcs and circles kept as true arcs. Lines, arcs, circles, ellipses, polylines, splines and blocks are read; text, dimensions and hatches are left out, and outlines that do not close too - the message says how many. Set the thickness in the properties. Add geometry: Drop STL, OBJ, 3MF, STEP, SVG, PNG or JPG files in the window or click to choose a file. Imported meshes can be turned, moved, cut with holes and built upon. A STEP file with several solids, an assembly from another CAD program, comes in as one body each under the name the file gives it, in its place to the others and in the colour the file gives it; several bodies under one entry of the file, the screws of a part say, become a part each. Its groups are not taken over yet. An SVG comes in as a sketch body, one from a tracer such as picsvg.com or Inkscape's "Trace Bitmap" as well: its outlines become the lines and curves of a sketch, 4 mm high and reading from above as in the drawing. In the properties you set its “Preenchimento”, an area or a stroke outside, inside or centred, and “Silhueta (sem furos)” leaves the holes out, see Sketches, "Fill and silhouette". You change the points themselves in sketch mode. If it should come in at a size of your own, type the width in the import window under SVG and picture: width in mm first, as in Tinkercad: the drawing is scaled to it, height and depth with it, and the field is empty again after that one import; left empty, an SVG comes in at its own size and a picture 50 mm wide. Only a very intricate SVG with more than 2500 lines and curves comes in as a fixed mesh. A PNG or JPG picture is traced into an outline and comes in the same way, as a sketch body 50 mm wide that you can resize afterwards: the part of the picture that is not its background, the background being the part that takes up more of the picture's edge. An SVG that holds nothing but one picture is traced the same way. A shape that cannot be built into a solid, such as an outline that crosses itself or touches itself at a point, is left out, and after the import PrintCaddy says how many there were. Then it helps to join overlapping pieces in the drawing program, close the outlines and save the file again. Drawings made on one page, such as the layers of one document exported as separate files, line up again when you switch on “SVG: manter o lugar na página do desenho” in the import window before you import them: each keeps its place on the page, where otherwise each is centred on itself. An SVG drawn in several colours comes in as one body per colour as well, each in its colour and in its place; with more than 12 colours, as a traced picture has, it stays one body. A coloured OBJ or 3MF comes in as one body per colour, each in its place. In an OBJ the colours sit either in the file itself, as in an OBJ from PrintCaddy, or in an .mtl beside it. Select that one too, or import the whole ZIP the way Tinkercad hands out its OBJ. A 3MF carries its colours itself, and in a project from Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer or PrusaSlicer each part takes the colour of its filament. A 3MF with several objects, such as a project with one object per plate, comes in as one body per object; modifiers, negative volumes and support blockers from the slicer are left out. Colour painted onto faces in the slicer is not read. From Tinkercad: An STL or OBJ export from Tinkercad comes in as geometry like any other mesh, and an OBJ keeps the colours. The real shapes come across with a free tool from the community: Export to PrintCaddy by taylormadearmy, a bookmark that converts a Tinkercad design in your browser into a .lyl file, which you open here with “Abrir projeto do PrintCaddy”. It is not part of PrintCaddy and we have not tested it ourselves yet; its author tested it on Windows with Chrome. A design saved with a newer PrintCaddy may hold things your version does not know yet, such as a new shape, a new setting or fonts of one's own. If PrintCaddy cannot open it for that reason, the message names both versions. If it opens, the notice says that newer things may look different here. Either way, reloading the page helps: the public site always serves the newest version. The installed app picks it up the next time it starts; on your own server you install the update. Template pictures are added in sketch mode, see Sketches.

A scanned or sculpted mesh often has far more triangles than its shape needs, and every one of them is carried along while you move, cut and save. “Simplificar malha” in the Modify group (or in the right-click menu of the body) shows the mesh as it is next to what a chosen share of its triangles would leave of it; both views turn and zoom together with the mouse buttons of the workplane. Set how much to keep as a percentage or a number of triangles, and “Simplificar” takes the lighter mesh. The result is a plain mesh: for the result of a cut or merge, “Editar grupo” and its original parts are given up. Cutting, merging and intersecting an imported mesh is calculated in your browser, so the workspace settings limit how many triangles such a mesh may have (“Cortar malhas importadas de até”). A mesh above the limit is not processed, and the message names its triangle count; simplify the mesh first, or raise the limit if your computer can take it.

If PrintCaddy does something unexpected, save a “Relatar erro”: the link sits in the footer at the bottom, next to the forum. It is a ZIP file, because GitHub and many forums refuse a bare .lyl: inside are your design as a .lyl and a short text file with the version, browser, screen size, the last messages and any errors. The start page opens the ZIP like a backup, or you unpack it and open the .lyl. Nothing personal is in it. Attach the file to your post in the forum or on GitHub, so the problem can be followed with exactly your design. If PrintCaddy stops with an error, a window with the error message shows instead of a blank page. From it you can save the state of the design last stored in the browser as a .lyl file, go back to the overview, or start a new design. The error message from the window and the saved file help when you report it.

When PrintCaddy runs on your own computer or web server, it can offer a shared folder in which all users keep designs. The start page then holds the designs in two tabs, “Servidor” for the shared folder and one for this browser, each with the number of designs in it; the one with more designs comes first and is open. You create folders there, move designs by dragging and search across the whole folder. A design that lives there saves itself back to it. A design from this browser goes onto the server by dragging its card onto the “Servidor” tab, or with “Enviar para o servidor” in the card's menu. While the “Servidor” tab is open, “Criar novo projeto 3D” and “Restaurar backup” put the design into the server folder you have open, and “Fazer backup de tudo” packs every design of the server, in its folders, and its custom shapes into one ZIP file. The start page shows a design by its file name, so renaming a design, on its card or at the top of the editor, renames the file on the server too. Deleting a design or a folder removes it for good, together with its working copy in this browser. Custom shapes kept on the server sit in its folder Custom shapes, see Shapes. Two things make that quicker: “Enviar tudo para o servidor” on the start page puts every design of this browser on the server in one go, and ticking “Novos projetos no servidor” makes every new design start in the server folder, so it is saved there from the first change on. With the tick, everything else that makes a design starts there too: opening or importing a file, “Restaurar backup” (with the backup's folders), duplicating and taking a state from the history, each into the server folder you had open; “Nova pasta” on the start page then makes a folder on the server. A design made in the first moments waits until the server has answered. When new designs must always start on the server and this browser holds none of its own, the start page shows only the server's designs. The tick is kept in this browser. A design that cannot go - its name is taken on the server, say - stays in the browser, and the message says how many. The other export formats (STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP, SVG, PNG and the drawing) can go into the same folder: in the export window, “Salvar no servidor” writes the file next to your design, or into the folder you have open on the start page for a design that is not on the server. A program that shares the folder, such as a slicer in Docker, can open it from there. The file does not appear in the list of designs. If a file of that name is already there, the message says so, and pressing the button again replaces it. That is not simultaneous editing: whoever opens a file works on a copy of their own. If somebody else has changed the file in the meantime, PrintCaddy refuses to overwrite it. On the public site this function is not switched on. How to set it up on your own server is described in the README on GitHub.

Todas as teclas num só lugar, tiradas direto do programa, então a lista está sempre certa. Os atalhos funcionam enquanto o plano de trabalho estiver em foco. Enquanto você digita num campo, eles não atrapalham. No Mac, Cmd vale sempre que aqui aparece Ctrl. No editor, “Atalhos de teclado” na área “Ajuda” abre a mesma lista numa janela. O botão de impressora na janela (“Imprimir ou salvar como PDF”) imprime só a lista, em preto sobre branco, a lista inteira em um lado de uma folha A4 ou Carta, em três colunas, para deixar à mão como referência rápida. Na janela de impressão do navegador, você também pode salvar como PDF. A caixa no alto da janela pesquisa a lista: ela mantém só os atalhos cuja frase, grupo ou teclas contêm todas as palavras digitadas, então "arredondamento" ou "ctrl+z" deixa só essas linhas. Maiúsculas e acentos não importam, e uma única letra ou dígito encontra essa tecla e as palavras que começam com ela. O X no fim da caixa a esvazia; com a caixa vazia, a lista inteira volta. O botão de impressora imprime o que a janela mostra, então depois de uma pesquisa imprime só os atalhos encontrados. A janela de atalhos de teclado no editor.

Não acha uma ferramenta? Pressione Ctrl+K ou clique na lupa na área “Ajuda” e digite o que você procura: uma ferramenta ("arredondamento", "espelhar"), uma forma ("cilindro") ou um comando ("exportar", "desfazer"). Navegue com as setas e pressione Enter, ou clique na entrada. A pesquisa entende a palavra em português, em inglês e em alemão, e ignora maiúsculas e acentos: "aushoehlen" encontra “Vazar”. Cada entrada mostra as teclas que fazem o mesmo e a área da barra de opções onde ela fica, para você aprender onde está. Entradas em cinza não podem ser executadas agora, na maioria das vezes porque nada está selecionado. Elas continuam na lista para que a pesquisa ainda mostre onde a ferramenta fica. O guia que você está lendo também tem uma caixa de pesquisa, no topo de cada página: digite uma ou duas palavras e ela lista as seções que contêm todas elas, com as palavras encontradas destacadas. Clique numa delas, ou pressione Enter para a primeira, para ir direto até lá. O nome de uma forma adiciona essa forma ao plano de trabalho, como clicar nela no menu de formas. Com o campo vazio, a pesquisa de comandos lista no topo os comandos que você usou por último. O nome de um sólido do seu projeto encontra esse sólido e o seleciona, o que ajuda num projeto com muitas peças. Os sólidos só aparecem depois que você digita. A pesquisa de comandos também funciona no modo de esboço, com as ferramentas de esboço.

Não acha onde ler sobre um botão ou um campo? Deixe o programa levar você até lá. Clique no ponto de interrogação na área “Ajuda”, ou pressione Shift+F1. O ponteiro vira um ponto de interrogação, e o que estiver embaixo dele fica contornado. Clique num botão, num campo, numa chave, numa alça, numa área da barra de opções ou na barra de título de uma janela. O elemento não faz o que normalmente faz. Em vez disso, abre uma pequena janela com o nome do elemento, um resumo curto da parte deste guia que fala dele, até dois outros lugares que o mencionam e o botão “Abrir no guia”. A ajuda é sobre o elemento que você apontou, não sobre a janela inteira em volta dele. Um elemento sem nome próprio usa o mais próximo em volta dele; dentro de uma janela, ele recorre ao ponto de interrogação dessa janela. “Abrir no guia” abre o guia nessa seção numa nova aba. Na nova aba, a seção fica com um contorno colorido, do título até o fim, para você ver onde ela começa e termina. Se o guia não fala nada sobre o elemento, a janela diz isso e oferece “Pesquisar no guia”. Esc, ou o ponto de interrogação de novo, sai do modo. Numa tela sensível ao toque não existe passar o mouse por cima: um toque num elemento abre a janela na hora. A janela se move pela barra de título, como as outras janelas. O programa encontra a seção pelo nome do elemento (o texto de um botão, o nome de um campo), porque este guia usa os nomes dos botões exatamente como aparecem no programa. Ele procura na mesma pesquisa da caixa no topo de cada página do guia, no idioma que você está usando, e roda inteiramente no seu navegador.

How an AI assistant such as Gemini, Claude or Codex creates and changes shapes, groups them and takes pictures of the view in your open editor. PrintCaddy comes with an MCP server. MCP is a standard through which an AI assistant can use tools in other programs. With it an AI client such as Gemini, Claude or Codex sees an open editor tab and works in it: it creates shapes, changes dimensions, groups, cuts, rounds edges, reads out the scene and takes pictures of the view. You describe the part, the AI builds it, you watch and can step in at any moment. The bridge between AI client and editor runs locally on your computer. Keep in mind, though: what the AI reads, meaning the scene and the pictures of the view, goes to the provider of your AI client, like any other input there. Important: The MCP bridge exists in the development server that you start yourself on your computer. On the public site and in installations with static hosting it is switched off. A copy you host yourself, such as the Docker image on a NAS, can switch it on with an access token; see "A copy on a NAS or server" below.

Get PrintCaddy from GitHub and start it in the project folder with npm run dev. Node.js must be installed. On Windows the quick-start line in the README takes care of that. Open an editor tab, for example http://127.0.0.1:3000/?editor=1. You can leave that to the AI: when no editor is open, the first tool that needs one starts your browser with an editor and waits until it has connected. That works for a PrintCaddy on your own computer; a copy on a NAS or server needs you to open the editor. Set LAYERLING_MCP_OPEN_EDITOR=0 for the MCP server to switch it off. Connect your AI client to the MCP server. The client starts it itself with node scripts/layerling-mcp-server.mjs.

Nothing to install: the project brings a .mcp.json that registers the server, and the skill under .claude/skills/layerling-mcp-skill. Open the PrintCaddy folder in Claude Code and ask, for example: "Use the PrintCaddy MCP tools to list my open editors and inspect the scene."

Claude Desktop does not read project files. Enter the server in its own configuration. As a template use docs/mcp/claude-desktop-config.example.json in the project, replacing the script path with the absolute path on your computer. Then restart Claude Desktop.
Copy the skill from docs/skills/layerling-mcp-skill into your Codex skills folder, enter the server in your Codex configuration using docs/mcp/codex-config.example.toml, and restart Codex.

Antigravity auto-discovers the workspace skill in .agents/skills/layerling-mcp-skill. For Gemini CLI, copy the skill from docs/skills/layerling-mcp-skill into your global skills folder (~/.gemini/skills/), add the server to your settings using docs/mcp/gemini-config.example.json, and restart the client. The detailed instructions for each client are in the README on GitHub.

h: A copy on a NAS or server
t: A copy you host yourself can let an AI client drive its open editors over the network. It is off by default, because whoever can drive the bridge can read and change the open designs. On the server, set LAYERLING_MCP_REMOTE to true and LAYERLING_MCP_TOKEN to a secret of at least 16 characters (for the Docker image in environment: of the compose file; no rebuild needed). Open an editor tab of that copy and keep it open, and give the MCP client the address and the same token: LAYERLING_URL=http://nas:3000 and LAYERLING_MCP_TOKEN=<the token>. Only a client with the token can list or drive the editors. The editor pages need none, but they only count under an address or name that only your own network can use (an IP address, a name without a dot, or one ending in .local or .lan); a real domain behind a reverse proxy goes into LAYERLING_MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS. Use it on a network you trust, and HTTPS beyond it. The README has the details.

The AI works with the same functions as you, through the same path as your operation in the editor. New PrintCaddy functions get their MCP action right away. workplane on a side of a body or back on the base plate, and hides or shows it layerling_capture_image takes a picture of the view: front, top, side, diagonally from a corner and more That lets the AI check itself: it creates something, takes a picture, looks and improves.

You say: "Build me a round box 60 mm across, 40 mm high with a 2.5 mm wall, open at the top, plus a flat lid with 'Tea' written in an arc." The AI creates the cylinders, hollows one, puts the curved text on the lid and takes pictures at the end to see whether it fits. Tip: Give the AI concrete dimensions and tell it what the part is for ("holder for a 12 mm rod, fits a Bambu Lab A1"). Then it makes more sensible decisions. And watch it build: you can step in yourself at any time, because it is the same editor.

c: Instalação como app, uso offline e hospedagem própria
t: Como abrir o PrintCaddy como um programa comum, mesmo sem rede, e como rodá-lo no seu próprio computador.

c: Instalação como app, uso offline e hospedagem própria
t: PrintCaddy pode ser instalado como um programa comum. Ele ganha então um ícone e uma janela próprios, sem barra de endereços. Depois da primeira visita, ele abre mesmo sem internet. Seus projetos continuam no seu computador. Vale a pena instalar: o app abre mais rápido (porque não precisa ser carregado de novo toda vez), funciona sem internet e alivia o servidor. Você não perde nada, já que o PrintCaddy continua avisando quando sai uma versão nova. Isso também protege os seus projetos: o Safari no Mac, no iPhone e no iPad apaga os dados guardados de um site que não é visitado há sete dias, mas não os de um app instalado. Se o seu navegador permitir, aparece na página inicial uma dica com “Instalar agora”. Caso contrário: Chrome e Edge: clique no ícone de instalação à direita da barra de endereços, ou escolha "Instalar como app" no menu do navegador. Safari no Mac: menu "Arquivo", depois "Adicionar ao Dock". Safari no iPhone e no iPad: ícone de compartilhar, depois "Adicionar à Tela de Início". Firefox: não instala apps. Mesmo assim, o PrintCaddy abre offline numa aba. Você pode fechar a dica na página inicial com “Ocultar esta dica”. No Chrome ou no Edge, abrir o app instalado uma segunda vez traz a janela já aberta para a frente, em vez de abrir outra. No computador, o PrintCaddy instalado no Chrome ou no Edge também se registra como programa para arquivos .lyl: no gerenciador de arquivos, um clique duplo num projeto abre o projeto no PrintCaddy, e Ctrl+S salva de volta nesse arquivo. No Android isso não funciona, porque lá o navegador não associa arquivos a web apps instalados; abra o projeto com “Abrir um projeto ou importar geometria” na página inicial.

c: Instalação como app, uso offline e hospedagem própria
t: Quando existe uma versão mais nova, o PrintCaddy mostra isso na página inicial. Em “Notas da versão e download” você lê o que mudou. O número da versão fica no canto inferior direito. Depois de recarregar a página, você está na versão nova. No the public site e em outros servidores web, uma página aberta percebe sozinha que há uma atualização. De tempos em tempos, sempre que você volta para a aba e logo que a página não encontra um arquivo do programa de que precisa, ela pergunta ao servidor qual é a versão. Se algo novo foi instalado nesse meio-tempo, um cartão no canto inferior direito avisa e lista as novidades. “Salvar e recarregar” primeiro grava no navegador o projeto que está aberto e depois carrega a página de novo; o projeto volta do jeito que você deixou. “Depois” adia o cartão por 15 minutos. Recarregue logo: uma página que fica na versão antiga pode carregar partes da nova que não combinam com ela. O mesmo cartão aparece quando isso já aconteceu: os módulos de cálculo de CAD, que só carregam quando você precisa deles pela primeira vez, informam de qual versão são. Se não for a da própria página (depois de uma atualização, ou com uma cópia guardada de uma versão antiga), o cartão pede que você recarregue antes que os dois deixem de se entender. Quando o PrintCaddy está aberto em várias abas, elas cuidam umas das outras: se outra aba já roda uma versão mais nova, na parte de baixo da aba antiga, um aviso pede que você a recarregue. E se o mesmo projeto estiver aberto em duas abas, as duas avisam, porque salvam automaticamente e uma sobrescreveria a outra. Se você abrir o PrintCaddy em mais uma aba enquanto já há uma aberta, a nova aba sugere continuar na antiga e se oferece para fechar. Se você quiser duas abas de propósito, por exemplo para dois projetos lado a lado, clique em “Continuar trabalhando aqui” na nova aba. Este guia também abre numa aba própria: enquanto o PrintCaddy estiver aberto ao lado, o botão do guia, no canto superior direito, diz "Voltar ao editor" e fecha o guia, em vez de abrir o editor uma segunda vez.

c: Instalação como app, uso offline e hospedagem própria
t: Você escolhe o idioma no canto superior direito, na lista de idiomas. O esquema de cores ao lado oferece “Sistema” (segue o sistema operacional), “Claro”, “Escuro” e “Grafite”, um cinza-escuro neutro.

c: Instalação como app, uso offline e hospedagem própria
t: PrintCaddy é software livre (AGPL-3.0) e pode rodar no seu próprio computador ou servidor, por exemplo numa oficina, num clube ou numa escola. Há várias formas, descritas no README no GitHub: O início rápido no Windows: uma única linha no PowerShell instala tudo e põe um atalho na área de trabalho. Se o PrintCaddy já estiver rodando, outro clique duplo não inicia um segundo servidor, só abre a página. Docker: para NAS (dispositivos de armazenamento em rede) e servidores domésticos, sem precisar instalar o Node.js. Cada versão sai como uma imagem pronta henmedia/layerling no Docker Hub (também ghcr.io/henmedia/layerling) para amd64 e arm64; docker run -d -p 3000:3000 -v layerling-thumbnails:/app/.codex/project-thumbnails henmedia/layerling:latest inicia o PrintCaddy, e num NAS você procura a imagem no registro do gerenciador de contêineres. O volume layerling-thumbnails mantém as miniaturas da página inicial quando você atualiza; sem ele, elas somem toda vez que o contêiner é criado de novo, até você abrir o projeto. Exportação estática: o resultado são arquivos simples que qualquer servidor web consegue servir. Eles precisam ficar na raiz de um endereço (https://layerling.example.com/ ou http://192.168.0.5:8080/), não numa subpasta nem abertos direto do disco; o README traz o passo a passo. Se o servidor tiver PHP e houver uma pasta store gravável ao lado do index.html, a exportação também passa a ser o armazenamento compartilhado de projetos. A ponte MCP para assistentes de IA só existe no servidor de desenvolvimento; veja Construindo com uma IA.

Working with fingers or a stylus: selecting several bodies, turning and zooming the view, the long press menu, and what to know on an iPad.

PrintCaddy runs in the browser of a tablet, and as an app from its home screen. A finger does what the left mouse button does. Three things a tablet does not have, a right mouse button, a Shift key and a wheel, have a way of their own: You want to On a tablet Select a body Tap it. Select several bodies Tap a body: a round button appears in the lower left. Tap it, and every further body you tap joins the selection; a tap on a selected body takes it out again. A tap on empty space changes nothing; a second tap on the button ends it and clears the selection. Or hold a finger still for half a second, choose “Selecionar vários”, then tap one body after another. Select all bodies Hold a finger still on empty space for half a second, choose “Selecionar tudo”. Open the menu of a right click Hold a finger still on a body or on empty space for half a second. Move a body Drag it. Resize, turn or lift a body Drag its handles, the small squares and arrows around it. A finger catches them from a little beside. Turn the view One finger on empty space, or drag the view cube. Zoom the view Two fingers: spread to come closer, pinch to go away. Move the view Slide two fingers together. Clear the selection Tap empty space. Not while “Girar a vista com um dedo” is on, where one finger turns the view; and in “Selecionar vários” the first tap on empty space only ends the mode and leaves the selection as it is, the next one clears it.

Without a Shift key, “Selecionar vários” in the menu of a long press does what Shift+click does on a computer. While it is on, a message says so, and each tap on a body adds it to the selection or takes it out again. A tap on empty space, or Esc on a keyboard, ends it and leaves the selection as it is. A finger on empty space still turns the view meanwhile. Then “Grupo de união”, “Alinhar” or a move work on all the bodies you picked. The same menu has “Colocar sobre uma face”, the key C for a touch screen. The selection then follows the finger over the faces of other bodies; a tap sets it down on the face you tap, even a sloped one, and the first tap is enough. The menu entry is also found by searching for "set down" or "cruise" (the command search, Ctrl+K on a keyboard).

One finger on empty space turns the view, two fingers zoom and move it. A finger that starts on a body works on the body, not on the view. If you would rather have it turn the view, switch on “Girar a vista com um dedo” in the camera bar: one finger then turns the view instead of selecting, wherever it starts. That switch only shows on a device with a touch screen. The view cube in the top left turns the view when you drag it, and a tap on one of its sides, corners or edges jumps to that view. See View and workplane.

h: Handles, small points and a stylus
t: A fingertip covers what it aims at. PrintCaddy lets a finger reach a little further to handles, points, lines and edges than a mouse pointer does, but a stylus is finer. This holds for a pen the tablet knows as a pen, such as an Apple Pencil or an S Pen. A plain stylus with a rubber tip counts as a finger for the screen and is not finer than one, so work with it as with a finger. An Apple Pencil that hovers above the screen on an iPad also shows the name of a control after a moment, in a small bubble, as the mouse pointer does with a tooltip. If bodies slip when children or hurried hands touch them, switch on “Selecionar antes de mover” in the settings: a body then has to be selected first, and only the next drag moves it.

Install it as an app. In Safari, tap the Share icon and choose "Add to Home Screen". The app opens in a window of its own without the address bar, and it works without a connection, see Offline and install. Your designs live in the browser (unless you host PrintCaddy yourself and set up a server folder). There is no account, and nothing is uploaded. Safari has a rule of its own against tracking: it deletes what a website stored after seven days in which you did not visit it in Safari. A web app added to the Home Screen is exempt from that rule, as WebKit documents it. That is one more reason to use the app from the Home Screen, and to back up important work: “Fazer backup de tudo” on the start page packs all designs into one file. Files. Safari lets a page write into a file only through a download, so “Exportar” puts the file into the Downloads of the Files app, and Ctrl+S on a keyboard downloads it again; see Files and saving. No keyboard needed. Every tool has a button in the ribbon, and a number field opens the on-screen keyboard. A keyboard on the iPad adds the keyboard shortcuts. A value box beside a body opens its number field with the second tap: the first tap only marks it, so a finger that lands on it by accident does not raise the keyboard.

Fingers and rubber-tip styluses work alike here. Two settings make a class easier: “Selecionar antes de mover” so that a touch does not move a body by accident, and “Girar a vista com um dedo” so that one finger always turns the view. The question mark button in the Help group of the ribbon switches on the “Ajuda interativa”: a tap on any button, field or handle then explains it, and the same button, or Esc, leaves it. For a whole class, switch on “Modo simplificado” in the settings. The ribbon then keeps only the tools a workshop uses (copy, paste, duplicate, delete, undo, group, mirror, chamfer, fillet, hollow, align, export), the shape library a short list, the buttons are larger, and the start page shows the designs and nothing else: no news, no welcome text, no help buttons and no links out of PrintCaddy. Switching it on is a tap; switching it off is a press held for two seconds on the button that then takes its place. A link ending in ?mode=simple switches it on for the device that opens it, ?mode=full switches it off again. Whoever runs PrintCaddy on a server can start everyone in it with LAYERLING_SIMPLE_MODE=true, or fix it for everyone with always, so that the program has no switch to leave it; see the README.
